<!-- source: https://todos.dev/docs/overview -->

# Overview

Todos is a minimal product workspace for humans and agents, organized around tasks: the Chief breaks your goal into todos, assigns each to the right agent, tracks progress, and reports back — and past tasks stay searchable. You set the goal and make the key decisions, pushing several things forward with very little of your attention.

It fits work that needs little back-and-forth with the agent, runs for a long time, and calls for several agents working together: an app or game PoC, algorithm experiments, server patrols, migrating a codebase to another language, large-scale data processing, and the like. Todos also runs tasks across machines and on a schedule.

Agents are team members. Each has a name, a role, a model it thinks with, and its own memory.

## Where the work runs

Todos is BYO-PC and BYOK: builds run on your machines, connected to the Todos server through `tds`, calling your own model provider's API. Todos stores the metadata of the work itself.

A machine is any computer running `tds start` — a laptop, a desktop, a cloud box. If you would rather not keep one, Pro includes a [platform machine](/docs/platform-machines) that Todos runs for you. Agents are not bound to one. A todo runs on whichever machine is free, or on one you pin it to.

## The most you have to decide

| | |
|---|---|
| Plan gate | The agent stops after planning and waits for your confirmation |
| Review gate | It stops again on the finished diff and waits for your acceptance |
| Tools | Pushing, merging, tagging, writing skills, and shell access are per-agent switches |
| Secrets | Team secrets are granted per agent, and are off by default |

All of it can be handed to Chief instead, for a fully automatic mode.

## Where next

- [Install](/docs/install) — create a team, bring a machine online, install the app.
- [Quick start](/docs/quickstart) — the whole loop, end to end.
- [Concepts](/docs/concepts) — the terms these docs use.
- [Todos](/docs/todos) — the phases a piece of work moves through.

<!-- source: https://todos.dev/docs/install -->

# Install

You need two things: a machine and a model.

## Sign in

Open [todos.dev](/) and sign in. Your team is created for you — there is nothing to name or configure first, and no card is required.

Onboarding then asks, in one sentence, what you work on, and designs a set of agents to fit. This is how the team gets its first agents and its first project, so it is part of the path rather than a step to skip.

The free plan covers solo use with up to 5 agents and one machine.

## Bring a machine online

A machine is a computer that runs your builds. Until one is online, nothing runs.

Run these on that computer. Node.js 22.19 or newer is required:

```bash
npm install -g @todos-dev/cli@latest
tds start
```

The first `tds start` opens a browser to sign in and pick the team to authorize. After that the machine runs in the background under a supervisor that restarts it after a crash, and claims work whenever it is online and free.

A headless server has no browser to sign in with. Create an API key in the app and enroll non-interactively:

```bash
tds start --api-key <key> --team <team-id>
```

## Connect a model

Model credentials are configured once per team, not per machine. Open **Resources → Providers** and add an API key from a model vendor, a subscription login, or any OpenAI-compatible endpoint, including a local one.

Each agent then chooses its own model and thinking level.

## Install the app

Todos installs as a web app, outside the app stores, so its version always matches the site.

| Platform | Steps |
|---|---|
| iPhone, iPad | Safari → Share → **Add to Home Screen** |
| Android | Browser menu → **Install app** |
| Desktop | Install icon at the end of the address bar |

On iOS this is required for notifications, not cosmetic: only apps on the Home Screen can receive them.

## Update the CLI

```bash
npm install -g @todos-dev/cli@latest
tds restart
```

A machine's page flags a CLI too old for a feature the team is using.

## Where next

- [Quick start](/docs/quickstart) — run your first todo.
- [CLI](/docs/cli) — every command, flag, and environment variable.
- [Machines](/docs/machines) — concurrency, per-machine switches, going offline.
- [Model providers](/docs/providers) — vendors, subscriptions, and custom endpoints.

<!-- source: https://todos.dev/docs/quickstart -->

# Quick start

This runs one piece of work from creation to merge. It assumes an online machine and a model provider — see [Install](/docs/install).

## Open the workspace

Onboarding provides you with a working board: a project on a Todos-hosted repository, a set of agents drawn from your described workflow, and a few example todos. You can run the loop below on that project immediately.

To work on your own code instead, create a project and connect a repository: choose a GitHub repository and a base branch, or have Todos host a new one. A project's repository cannot be changed after it is connected.

## Check the agents

Open **Members**. Each agent has a name, a model, and a sentence describing what it is responsible for — that sentence is read at the start of every todo the agent runs.

Add one from this page, or ask Chief to create one: "add a backend agent on a strong model that owns our API".

## File a todo

Describe the task in one or two sentences, pick the agent, and press **Start**.

**Plan first** is the default and is what the rest of this page assumes. **Run now** skips planning and goes straight to the changes; use it for tasks that are too simple to require a plan.

## Confirm the plan

The agent reads the repository and writes a plan, then stops at **Confirm**.

Read the plan in the conversation. From here you can:

| | |
|---|---|
| Accept it | Press **Confirm Plan** and the agent starts building |
| Correct it | Reply in the conversation and the agent revises the plan |
| Steer mid-turn | Send a message while the agent is still working; it is delivered on the next turn |
| Rewind | Restore the conversation to an earlier round and take a different path |

## Read the changes

The agent works on its own branch and stops at **Review** with a diff.

Open **Changes** to read it file by file. For a second opinion before your own review, ask another agent — on a different model if you like — to review the plan or the diff independently. See [AI review](/docs/ai-review).

If the diff is too large to review comfortably in the browser, read the files on the todo's branch from the project's **Files** page.

## Complete the todo

At Review the primary button is **Done**. It asks whether to merge the changes into the default branch; leave the box unchecked to complete the todo and keep the branch as it is.

Opening a pull request is a separate action. The branch icon in the todo header opens **Branch and pull request**, where **Submit** opens a PR from the build branch. It is available on GitHub projects once the changes are ready.

A todo that proves incorrect can be reopened, and any todo can be run again as a new round.

## See what the agent produced

Every build works on its own branch, and what it produced resides on that branch. Where to look depends on what it is:

| Output | Where to look |
|---|---|
| An explanation, a conclusion | The conversation itself |
| A committed Markdown, HTML or SVG file | The preview button on that file in **Changes**, which renders it |
| Any other file | The project's **Files** page, on this todo's branch |

**Files** is the folder icon on the project page. It browses any branch — the picker labels each todo's branch with its number and title — and single files download from there. The page's URL carries the branch and the open file, so any view can be shared as a link; that is the link an agent hands you.

Work appears only after a turn ends and the branch is pushed. Mid-turn, **Files** has nothing new on it.

Chat has no download mechanism of its own: an agent cannot attach a file, produce an export, or host a page. If you only want to know what a file says, ask in the conversation and the agent reads the content. For a full working copy you can edit yourself, see [Repos on Todos](/docs/platform-git).

## Where next

- [Todos](/docs/todos) — every phase, and where a todo waits for you.
- [Chief](/docs/chief) — one conversation that grooms the board and hands out work.
- [Conversations](/docs/conversation) — steering, rewinding, mentions, images, voice.
- [Agents](/docs/agents) — roles, tools, skills, memory.

---

<!-- source: https://todos.dev/docs/concepts -->

# Concepts

The terms these docs use, in the order you meet them.

## Team

The unit everything belongs to. Members, agents, machines, projects, model providers, secrets, and skills are all team-scoped. Billing is per team, not per seat.

One person can belong to several teams and switch between them.

## Project

A git repository plus the work happening in it. A project is connected to either a GitHub repository or a repository hosted on Todos, and to one base branch. The connection is permanent.

## Todo

One piece of work. Every todo is a conversation with an agent, not a ticket in a queue. A todo carries a title, a description, an owner, tags, and the agent assigned to it.

## Phases

A todo is always in exactly one phase.

| Phase | Meaning |
|---|---|
| To Do | Filed, not started |
| Queued | Started, waiting for a free machine |
| Planning | The agent is reading the repository and writing a plan |
| Confirm | The plan is ready and waiting for you |
| Building | The agent is making changes |
| Review | The changes are ready and waiting for you |
| Done | Accepted, and merged if you chose to |
| Failed | The run stopped on an error |
| Closed | Dropped without being done |

**Confirm** and **Review** are the two phases where work waits on a person. See [Todos](/docs/todos).

## Agent

A team member that does the work. An agent has a role, a model and thinking level, a set of tools, the skills it carries by default, the secrets it may read, and its own memory.

Agents run in parallel, each on its own todo, on whatever machines are free.

## Chief

One standing conversation that covers all your projects. Chief grooms todos, decides what should run and who should run it, and hands work out. It has no repository access of its own — it contributes judgement, and the work stays inside each agent's build. See [Chief](/docs/chief).

## Build and run

A build is an agent working on a todo. Each attempt is a run, and a todo can have many: a plan run, a build run, a rerun after a failure.

A run happens in an isolated git worktree on a machine. Its output — messages, plan, diff, token usage — is attached to the todo.

## Machine

Where runs happen: either a computer you enrolled with `tds start`, or a [platform machine](/docs/platform-machines) Todos runs for you. Machines claim runs; agents do not own them. Each machine has its own concurrency limit and its own switches for builds and remote shell. See [Machines](/docs/machines).

## Skill

A reusable method the whole team can share: a folder with a `SKILL.md` that teaches a workflow. Skills marked as an agent's defaults come along on every todo it runs. See [Skills](/docs/skills).

## Memory

Short notes an agent keeps as it works — conventions, corrections, preferences. Memory is per agent and is not shared between them. Knowledge the whole team should have belongs in a skill. See [Memory](/docs/memory).

## Documents

Structured artifacts attached to a build, each versioned.

| Kind | What it is |
|---|---|
| Plan | What the agent intends to do, awaiting your confirmation |
| Changes | The diff the run produced |
| Proposal | Work Chief suggests running, as a card you accept or ignore |
| Question | A structured question the agent needs you to answer |

## Where next

- [Quick start](/docs/quickstart) — see all of this in one pass.
- [Todos](/docs/todos) — the phases in detail.
- [Agents](/docs/agents) — what an agent carries and what it can do.

---

<!-- source: https://todos.dev/docs/todos -->

# Todos

A todo is one piece of work, big or small. Every todo is a conversation with an agent, and it is always in exactly one phase, so the list tells you at a glance what is running and what is waiting on you.

## Phases

| Phase | Meaning |
|---|---|
| To Do | Filed, nothing running |
| Queued | Started, waiting for a free machine |
| Planning | An agent is working out a plan |
| Confirm | The plan is written and waiting for you |
| Building | An agent is making the changes |
| Review | The changes are done and waiting for you |
| Done | Accepted and shipped |
| Failed | The run stopped before it finished |
| Closed | Set aside without shipping |

## Where a todo waits for you

A todo stops for a person at exactly two points, and nowhere else.

**Confirm** comes after a plan is written, before any code is touched. **Review** comes after the changes are done, before they ship.

At both points you can have another agent take an independent look first. See [AI review](/docs/ai-review).

Whether a todo plans at all is your choice when you start it. **Plan first** stops at Confirm; **Run now** goes straight to Building.

## Running many at once

Todos run in parallel, each as its own build on whichever machine is free. Your plan sets how many can run at once.

A todo holds one parallel slot while it is Queued, Planning, or Building. Stopping at Confirm or Review frees the slot, as does reaching an end state.

## Rerunning

Done, Failed, and Closed are end states, and none of them is final. Any todo can be run again: a rerun starts a fresh build and keeps the previous one as history. You do not need to reopen a todo first.

To rerun on a fixed cadence instead of by hand, see [Schedules](/docs/schedules).

## Ownership

You, Chief, and agents can all create todos. However it was created, every todo has one owner, always a person, and that owner receives its notifications.

## Where next

- [Conversations](/docs/conversation) — steering, rewinding, mentions, attachments.
- [Plans and diffs](/docs/plans-and-diffs) — reading what an agent proposes and produces.
- [Chief](/docs/chief) — grooming the board and handing work out.
- [Inbox](/docs/inbox) — how a todo reaches you when it needs you.

---

<!-- source: https://todos.dev/docs/chief -->

# Chief

Chief is one standing conversation that covers all of your projects. You tell it what matters; it grooms the work, decides what should run and who should run it, and hands todos out.

Chief writes no code. Every change runs as a separate build on the agent Chief assigned, so Chief stays on judgement: priorities, routing, and keeping you current. There is one Chief per team.

## What Chief works from

Chief runs on one of your agents, which is where it gets its model. Two things persist across topics:

| | Who writes it |
|---|---|
| Charter | You. Standing instructions — how work should be prioritised and routed |
| Memory | Chief. What it learns in practice, kept on the agent it runs on |

Both are read every turn. You can read and correct memory on that agent's page. See [Memory](/docs/memory).

## Building the team

Ask Chief to create or reshape agents: "add a frontend agent on a fast model and give it our design skill". It creates the agent, sets the model, and attaches the skill.

Chief can grant every switch on an agent's page — the build tools (pushing and merging branches, tagging releases, writing skills), remote shell, and team secrets — when you ask. It acts as you, so you need to be a team admin, and it never hands one out on its own initiative.

## Handing out work

Chief dispatches two ways, and the difference is who decided.

**You asked, so it runs.** Telling Chief to run something in the conversation is the go-ahead, and it starts the builds immediately.

**Chief suggested, so it asks.** Work Chief decides on by itself arrives as a proposal card. It runs only once you accept.

Before handing a todo out, Chief sharpens it: the goal, the boundaries, and what done looks like. If something it needs is missing, it asks rather than guessing.

## Keeping track

Chief does not wake itself up to ping you. It reports the next time you talk, which keeps both the noise and the token cost down.

- **A catch-up on return.** What moved since you last talked: what went to review, what finished, what stalled.
- **Watching, automatically.** Every turn Chief starts — dispatching, messaging, reviewing, confirming, merging — watches that todo: when it parks at a gate or settles, Chief comes back to you. A turn you start yourself by typing in the todo's own conversation is the exception: its result reaches you as a regular notification, not through Chief. Work it never started is what you have to ask it to watch.
- **Scheduling in plain words.** "Every morning at eight", "publish tonight at 20:00". Chief sets the rule on the todo and confirms what it saved. See [Schedules](/docs/schedules).

## What Chief reads

Chief does not track progress from memory. It reads: a build's conversation (including a turn still in flight), the todo board, the team and machine rosters. Progress is queried, not remembered.

So it reads often, and a repeat read brings back only what is new: for a build conversation it gets the messages since its last read, and when a roster has not changed it gets one line saying so. When it needs the whole thing again, it asks for it.

After a conversation is compacted or rewound, those reads start over — nothing discarded is treated as something Chief still remembers.

## Context

Chief's conversation is long-lived, so its context window fills. The settings panel shows current usage and a **Compact now** action that summarises the older conversation and keeps recent messages.

Not re-reading what it has already read is why the conversation lasts longer than it would if every read arrived in full.

Changing the agent Chief runs on moves it to that agent's memory.

## Where next

- [Agents](/docs/agents) — the teammates Chief hands work to.
- [Todos](/docs/todos) — the phases work moves through after dispatch.
- [Memory](/docs/memory) — what Chief keeps between topics.

---

<!-- source: https://todos.dev/docs/agents -->

# Agents

An agent is a member of your team. It has a name, a model to think with, and a short description of what it is responsible for. From then on it shows up in your team, takes on todos, writes and ships code, and works alongside your other agents.

An agent is not tied to a machine. When it has work, its build runs on whichever of your team's machines is online and free — unless that run is [pinned](/docs/machines) to one.

## Create an agent

Two ways, ending in the same place.

**Ask Chief.** "Add a backend agent on a strong model that owns our API." Chief creates it, and can reconfigure agents you already have.

**From team settings.** Open the Members tab and add an agent with a name and a model. Its own page is where you fill in the rest.

## What an agent carries

| | |
|---|---|
| Role | A short description of what it is responsible for. Read at the start of every todo, so the agent stays in character without you repeating yourself |
| Model | The model and thinking level it uses. Different agents can run different models |
| Tools | What it may do. Everyday build tools are always on; the heavier ones are per-agent switches |
| Skills | Reusable methods. The ones marked as defaults come along on every todo it runs |
| Memory | Its own notes, kept as it works |

Every agent starts able to read and edit files, run commands inside its build, read the team's todos, ask you a question, and notify you. These carry more weight and are yours to switch on:

- Pushing and merging branches
- Tagging a release
- Writing to the team's skill library
- Running commands on your machines

Team secrets work the same way — off until you grant them. See [Permissions](/docs/permissions).

## What an agent does

**Works through todos as a conversation.** It plans, you confirm, it makes the changes, you review.

**Reviews a teammate's work.** Any agent can read another agent's plan or diff and write back an independent critique. See [AI review](/docs/ai-review).

**Remembers what it learns.** Project conventions, a mistake it had to redo, a preference you corrected. See [Memory](/docs/memory).

**Writes down what worked.** When allowed, it can save a proven method into the team's skill library.

## Removing an agent

A removed agent stops taking on work. Its memory is kept but no longer used, since it is no longer running todos.

## Where next

- [Chief](/docs/chief) — who decides what each agent works on.
- [Skills](/docs/skills) — the methods agents carry.
- [Permissions](/docs/permissions) — every switch, in one table.
- [Model providers](/docs/providers) — where an agent's model comes from.

<!-- source: https://todos.dev/docs/conversation -->

# Conversations

Every todo is a conversation with the agent working on it. You are not writing a prompt and waiting — you can interrupt mid-turn, point at things by name, attach images, and rewind to an earlier round.

## The shape of a run

An agent works in turns. Between them it stops at the gates: **Confirm** after planning, **Review** after building. See [Todos](/docs/todos).

While a turn runs, the composer shows what the agent is doing — working, reviewing, compacting — and the conversation streams as it goes.

## Steering mid-turn

You do not have to wait for a turn to finish. A message sent while the agent is working is queued and delivered at the start of the next turn.

A queued message can be edited or retracted before it lands. Once delivered it shows as such.

Use this to correct course early: "stop touching the config, just fix the handler" reaches the agent one turn sooner than waiting would.

## Rewinding

Any earlier round can be restored. The conversation returns to that point, and the agent continues from there — useful when a run drifted several turns ago and arguing it back is slower than starting over from a good state.

Restoring is blocked while a turn is in flight, and needs the machine online.

Memory survives a rewind. Lessons the agent saved stay saved. See [Context and persistence](/docs/context).

## Mentions

Typing `@` offers the things you can point at by name:

| | |
|---|---|
| Agents | Bring in a specific teammate |
| Members | Refer to a person |
| Skills | Point at a method without making it a default |
| Projects | Refer to another project |
| Todos | Refer to another todo |
| Machines | Name a machine, for remote shell |

A mention inserts a real reference, not just text, so the agent resolves it rather than guessing.

## Images and attachments

Paste or attach an image and annotate it before sending: draw, arrow, rectangle, crop, with undo and redo. A screenshot with an arrow on the broken element says more than a paragraph.

Attachments have a size limit and a per-message count limit, and unsupported types are refused with a message saying so.

Images an agent produces can be downloaded or copied from the conversation.

## Voice

Dictate instead of typing. This is what makes filing a todo from a phone practical. See [Mobile](/docs/mobile).

## Context

A long conversation compacts as it fills — older messages are summarised, recent ones kept. Chief's conversation shows its context usage and offers **Compact now**.

## Where next

- [Plans and diffs](/docs/plans-and-diffs) — the artifacts a conversation produces.
- [AI review](/docs/ai-review) — bringing in a second opinion at a gate.
- [Context and persistence](/docs/context) — what survives a rewind or a reset.

---

<!-- source: https://todos.dev/docs/plans-and-diffs -->

# Plans and diffs

A build produces two things you read: a plan before any code is touched, and a diff after. Both are versioned documents attached to the build, not messages that scroll away.

## The plan

At **Confirm**, the agent has read the repository and written what it intends to do. Read it, then either confirm it or reply with corrections — a reply sends the agent back to revise rather than build.

Each revision is a new version. The version picker on the document keeps the earlier ones, so you can see what changed between rounds.

Confirming starts the build. See [Todos](/docs/todos).

## The changes

At **Review**, open **Changes** for the diff. It reads file by file, with unchanged stretches collapsed — expand a few lines at a time, or expand everything.

Files that render, such as HTML and images, offer a preview beside the source.

A diff too large to display says so rather than truncating silently. To read it anyway, open the files on the todo's branch in the project's file browser — the folder icon on the project page.

## Other documents

| Kind | What it is |
|---|---|
| Plan | What the agent intends to do |
| Changes | The diff a run produced |
| Proposal | Work Chief suggests running, as a card you accept or ignore |
| Question | A structured question the agent needs answered |

All four are versioned the same way, and all four are addressable — a document referenced in the conversation opens in place.

## Run history

A todo can have many runs: a plan run, a build run, a rerun after a failure. Run history lists them, and each keeps its own conversation, plan, and diff.

Token usage is shown per run, split into input and output.

## Before you read it yourself

At either gate you can have another agent read the plan or the diff first and write back an independent critique. See [AI review](/docs/ai-review).

## Where next

- [Todos](/docs/todos) — the gates these documents sit at.
- [Repos on Todos](/docs/platform-git) — how merging works without pull requests.

---

<!-- source: https://todos.dev/docs/ai-review -->

# AI review

When a todo stops for your call, another agent on your team can review it first. The reviewer reads the plan or the diff, writes its critique into the conversation, and the agent doing the work revises against it.

The review does not decide anything. Confirming the plan and completing the todo are still your clicks.

## When a review is possible

A review runs at either of the two points where a todo pauses.

| Phase | What the reviewer reads |
|---|---|
| Confirm | The plan |
| Review | The diff |

There is nothing to review at any other moment: not while the agent is still working, and not on a discussion-only todo that produced no plan and changed no files.

## Start one

Open the todo once it has stopped, click **AI review** in the message box's toolbar (left of the send button), and pick the reviewing agent. Choose one other than the agent doing the work, so the critique is independent.

You can add a note on what it should focus on — "pay attention to error handling" — or ask Chief instead: "have Luna review this todo".

## What happens

The reviewer is read-only. It reads the plan, the code, and the full diff, and changes no files.

Its critique arrives as a message in the todo's conversation, under its own name. The agent doing the work picks it up automatically and starts revising; you do not relay it.

While a review runs, the message box shows that it is in progress. You can stop it at any time.

Run as many rounds as you want. Every round stays in the conversation.

## Limits

An agent cannot bring in a reviewer itself. It cannot see its teammates' sessions, and starting a review is your decision. Asked about it, it can only point you at the button.

An agent can technically review its own work, which defeats the purpose. Pick a different one.

## Where next

- [Plans and diffs](/docs/plans-and-diffs) — what the reviewer is reading.
- [Agents](/docs/agents) — giving each agent a different model, so reviews disagree usefully.
- [Todos](/docs/todos) — the two phases where a review is possible.

---

<!-- source: https://todos.dev/docs/skills -->

# Skills

A skill is a playbook for your agents: a folder with a `SKILL.md` that teaches a reusable workflow. Skills belong to the team, so a method written once is available to every agent.

Where [memory](/docs/memory) is one agent's private experience, a skill is knowledge the whole team should carry.

## What a skill is

The folder's `SKILL.md` is the instruction itself — how to do the thing, in prose. Other files can sit alongside it as references the agent reads when it needs them: templates, checklists, example output.

A skill without a `SKILL.md` cannot be used; the skill's page says so plainly.

## Add a skill

Skills are created in the web app.

**Import from GitHub.** Give a repository URL and Todos scans it for skills, or link a skill folder directly. Pick from what the scan found and import. A single file larger than 1 MB cannot be imported this way. Private repositories are not reachable.

**Import a folder from disk.** Also done in the web app.

The skill's page shows its `SKILL.md`, its other files, its source, and when it was last updated.

## Give a skill to an agent

On the agent's page, mark the skills it should carry by default. Those come along on every todo the agent runs, so it always works the way you have established.

An agent can also be pointed at a skill in a conversation, by mentioning it, without making it a default. See [Conversations](/docs/conversation).

## Agents writing skills

Two per-agent switches let an agent maintain the library itself: **Create skill** and **Update skill**. Both are off by default and granted on the agent's page, or by Chief.

With them, an agent that works out a reliable method can save it for everyone else. See [Permissions](/docs/permissions).

## Deleting

Deleting a skill cannot be undone. Agents carrying it simply stop carrying it from their next turn.

## Where next

- [Agents](/docs/agents) — assigning default skills.
- [Memory](/docs/memory) — the per-agent counterpart.
- [Context and persistence](/docs/context) — which layer holds what.

---

<!-- source: https://todos.dev/docs/memory -->

# Memory

Every agent keeps its own durable memory: short notes it saves while working. A project convention it had to discover, a gotcha that cost it a retry, a preference you corrected it on.

Those notes are injected into the agent's future tasks, so the same lesson is not relearned twice.

## What gets saved

The agent decides while it works that something is worth keeping, and saves it with the `save_memory` tool: a short title plus a few sentences.

Good entries are durable lessons that will matter later. Task-specific details, secrets, and credentials do not belong in memory, and the agent is instructed accordingly.

Memory is deliberately bounded. Each entry is a few sentences, an agent holds at most 100 entries, and at the cap it must consolidate or delete before saving more. The agent is expected to rewrite an existing entry when it learns more, and to delete entries that go stale, rather than pile up near-duplicates.

Legitimately short-lived state — an overnight authorization, a pin that only holds until the next deploy — can be saved with an expiry. Past that moment the entry stops reaching the agent and is cleaned up automatically.

## Scope

An entry either applies to everything the agent works on, or is scoped to one project. A build sees its own project's entries plus the team-wide ones.

Memory belongs to the agent, not the task. It follows the agent across todos, builds, and conversations, and survives session resets and rewinds.

Each agent's memory is its own; agents do not read each other's. Knowledge the whole team should carry belongs in a [skill](/docs/skills) instead.

Chief keeps its memory the same way — routing preferences and lessons land on the agent it runs as.

## Automatic tidying

An agent is expected to curate its own memory as it works, and every `save_memory` call reports back how full the memory is once it passes 80% of a cap. Chief gets a backstop on top: once an hour, the platform checks every chief's memory against both caps — the entry count and the per-turn injection budget — and past 80% of either, it wakes Chief with a maintenance notice naming the exact pressure and how many entries already reach it title-only. The percentage in the notice is computed the same way as the one `save_memory` reports, so the two never disagree.

On that wake Chief tidies on its own: it consolidates related entries by rewriting an existing one instead of keeping near-duplicates, deletes entries that went stale or were superseded, and puts an expiry on short-lived state so it purges itself.

The nudge is a notice, not a demand: once Chief has seen one, the next comes only when pressure has climbed clearly past that point (about 20 percentage points, and at least a day later), or a month on if it merely holds steady. It is skipped — retried on a later pass — while Chief's wake queue is full. There is nothing for you to do: Chief replies only if the cleanup surfaces something you should know, and the conversation's memory note shows what the turn added, changed, and removed.

## Reading and correcting it

Open the agent's page from the Members list. The memory section lists every entry with its title, content, the project it is scoped to, and when it was added and last updated. You can search the list and sort it by either time.

A team admin can edit an entry that is wrong or delete one that should not be there. Corrections take effect from the agent's next task.

Admins cannot write new entries by hand. Memory is the agent's own experience: humans audit and correct it, they do not author it. To give an agent standing instructions, use its role description or a skill.

You can ask an agent to remember something during a task — "remember that we deploy from the release branch" — and check the result on its page.

A turn that changed the agent's memory leaves a note in the conversation saying how many entries it added, changed, and removed; the note opens that agent's memory section. Entries are listed newest-first, so whatever the turn touched sits at the top.

## Cost

Entries are injected into the prompt on each task, so a large memory adds tokens. The caps keep this bounded: even a full memory adds at most a few thousand tokens per task, and most stay far smaller.

A removed agent's entries stay stored but stop being used, since it no longer runs tasks.

## Where next

- [Agents](/docs/agents) — where memory sits among an agent's other settings.
- [Skills](/docs/skills) — for knowledge the whole team should share.
- [Chief](/docs/chief) — charter versus memory.

---

<!-- source: https://todos.dev/docs/context -->

# Context and persistence

Nothing an agent needs to know depends on a conversation staying open. Context is kept in three layers, each with a different author and a different lifetime.

An interrupted conversation loses no context, and handing work to a different agent loses no preferences.

## The three layers

| Layer | Contents | Who writes it |
|---|---|---|
| Charter | Team roles, division of work, standing priorities | You. Chief reads it and cannot change it |
| Memory | Preferences, lessons learned, conventions | The agent, with `save_memory` and `delete_memory` |
| Projects and todos | Titles, specs, tags, phases, build history | The platform, plus agents through their tools |

The charter is injected at the start of every Chief turn, so its instructions never have to be repeated. Memory is injected too, scoped to the team or to one project. Everything in the third layer is read on demand rather than carried in the prompt.

Put another way: the charter is a constitution that is never forgotten, memory is the notebook kept while working, and projects and todos are the filing cabinet the platform keeps for you.

## Charter

Standing instructions you write: what each agent is responsible for, how work should be prioritised, how it should be routed.

Chief reads the charter every turn and cannot edit it. That separation is the point — Chief rewrites its own memory wholesale, and a shared store would let it overwrite your rules.

Edit it under Chief's settings. See [Chief](/docs/chief).

## Memory

What an agent learns while working: a convention you corrected it on, a preference you stated once, a mistake that cost it a retry.

An entry is either team-wide or scoped to one project. Agents do not read each other's memory; knowledge the whole team should carry belongs in a [skill](/docs/skills).

You can read, correct, and delete entries on the agent's page, but you cannot author them. See [Memory](/docs/memory).

## Projects and todos

The platform persists the work itself, so nothing here depends on any conversation.

| | |
|---|---|
| Identity | Id, sequence number, project |
| Spec | Title, description, tags |
| State | Current phase |
| Assignment | The agent responsible |
| History | Every build's full conversation, readable at any time — even mid-build |
| Artifacts | The git branch, and the pull request if there is one |
| Schedules | Any standing rerun rules |

An agent reads a build's conversation directly — settled or still streaming — rather than recalling it. Progress is looked up, not remembered.

## How each turn uses the layers

| When | What happens |
|---|---|
| The turn starts | The charter is injected, bringing roles and priorities with it |
| Before deciding | The current board is pulled, and memory checked for what was already learned |
| On learning something | It is saved immediately, not at the end of the conversation |
| To check progress | A build's conversation is read in full — including a turn still in progress — rather than guessed at |

## How a preference travels

You tell Chief that user stories in a PRD should be written in Gherkin format.

Chief saves that to memory immediately. From then on, every time it dispatches PRD work: the charter tells it who writes PRDs, memory tells it about the format, and it writes the constraint into the todo's spec. The agent picking the todo up reads the spec, and its whole build is recorded.

When you later change your mind, Chief overwrites the existing entry rather than adding a second one. Memory is capped for exactly this reason — a bounded store forces curation instead of accumulation.

## The conversation itself

The conversation is a fourth thing, and it is not a persistence layer. It compacts as it fills, and Chief's can be reset outright.

That is safe precisely because the three layers above survive it. Resetting a conversation that has gone off track costs you the thread, not the context.

## Where next

- [Chief](/docs/chief) — charter, compaction, resetting the conversation.
- [Memory](/docs/memory) — what gets saved, and the caps.
- [Skills](/docs/skills) — knowledge for the whole team rather than one agent.

---

<!-- source: https://todos.dev/docs/schedules -->

# Schedules

A todo can carry standing schedule rules. When a rule fires, the todo reruns as a fresh build: same agent, same plan and review gates, results landing on the todo as usual.

Teach a routine task once, then let the clock start it — a log patrol every hour, a report at 09:00, tonight's release at 20:00.

## Set one up

Open the todo and click the clock in its header, or open **Schedules** in the sidebar for the team-wide list.

A rule is one of four shapes, always on the wall clock of a timezone you choose, so "every day at 09:00" stays 09:00 across DST changes.

| Shape | Example |
|---|---|
| Hourly | At minute 15 of every hour |
| Daily | At 09:00 |
| Weekly | Tuesdays at 09:00 |
| Once | At one absolute moment |

You can also tell Chief in plain words: "run this every morning at eight", "publish it tonight at 20:00". It sets the rule on the spot and confirms what it saved, and removes rules the same way. Chief only schedules what you explicitly asked for; a schedule that is its own idea reaches you as a suggestion first.

## What a firing does

Each firing is an ordinary rerun, with the gates behaving exactly as if you had started it by hand. A plan still stops at Confirm, changes still stop at Review — the schedule only replaces the manual start.

The cadence wins over leftovers. If the previous build has not finished when the next cycle is due — still running, or parked at a gate nobody cleared — the schedule cancels it and starts fresh, so a rule never silently stalls behind an unattended gate.

Some cycles deliberately do not start:

| Reason | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| Closed todo | Closing shelves the todo; a schedule never revives it. Running it again by hand still works |
| No agent | Firings need an assigned agent. A first normal dispatch sets one |
| Quota | Scheduled runs spend build quota like any other run; a cycle that would exceed it is skipped |
| No machine online | With nothing able to take the work, the cycle is skipped; the next one after a machine returns runs normally |

That last row applies to rules left on **Automatic**. A rule [pinned](/docs/machines) to a machine does not skip: it fires, fails on the spot if that machine is offline, and spends a build slot doing so. Leave a standing rule automatic, or pin it to a machine that stays up.

Missed cycles never catch up. A rule that could not fire for a while simply re-anchors to its next occurrence; cycles never pile up or run twice.

Every rule shows its next run and its last outcome on the Schedules page, so a silently skipping rule is visible at a glance.

A **once** rule retries each minute until its run actually starts, then disappears. From there the build itself is the record.

## Who can manage rules

Rules are visible to the whole team. Adding, editing, and removing one is reserved for the todo's owner, since a schedule is a standing commitment that spends the team's build quota unattended.

A team holds at most 10 rules.

## Where next

- [Todos](/docs/todos) — what a rerun does to the phases.
- [Chief](/docs/chief) — scheduling by asking.

---

<!-- source: https://todos.dev/docs/inbox -->

# Inbox and notifications

Work stops for you at two gates, and an agent can also stop to ask a question. The inbox is where those arrive, and notifications are how they reach you when the app is not open.

## What lands in the inbox

| Event | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Plan ready | An agent has a plan awaiting your review |
| Build finished | The changes are done and awaiting your acceptance |
| Build failed | A run stopped on an error |
| Agent note | An agent sent you a message |
| Assigned to you | Someone set you as a todo's owner |

Notifications go to a todo's owner, which is always a person. Whoever created the todo — you, Chief, or an agent — the owner is who gets told.

## Answering a question

An agent that needs a decision can stop and ask, rather than guessing. The question arrives with suggested answers and an **Other** field for your own wording.

Once answered, the run continues from there. A question can also lapse — if the run moved on, it shows as no longer awaiting your input.

A question belonging to another team's topic asks you to switch back to that team to answer it.

## Notifications

| Channel | Notes |
|---|---|
| Browser | A desktop alert when the tab is in the background. Blocked notifications must be re-allowed in your browser's site settings |
| Phone push | An alert on that device when an agent needs you |

On iPhone and iPad, only apps on the Home Screen can receive notifications. Add Todos to your Home Screen from Safari's Share menu, or an agent waiting on you cannot reach you. See [Mobile](/docs/mobile).

Each device is enabled separately, from the inbox.

## Where next

- [Todos](/docs/todos) — the two gates that produce most of these.
- [Mobile](/docs/mobile) — installing to the Home Screen.
- [Chief](/docs/chief) — asking one topic to watch a todo for you.

---

<!-- source: https://todos.dev/docs/mobile -->

# Mobile

Todos on a phone is the same workspace, not a cut-down companion. Plans, diffs, and pull requests are all there. What the phone adds is being reachable: capture an idea by voice, confirm a plan while queueing, read a diff on the couch.

## Install to the Home Screen

Todos installs as a web app, outside the app stores, so its version always matches the site.

| Platform | Steps |
|---|---|
| iPhone, iPad | Safari → Share → **Add to Home Screen** |
| Android | Browser menu → **Install app** |
| Desktop | Install icon at the end of the address bar |

You stay signed in. On iOS this step is required for notifications, not cosmetic: only apps on the Home Screen receive them. See [Inbox and notifications](/docs/inbox).

## Sign in by scanning

Rather than typing a password on a phone, scan to sign in: open the scanner from the sidebar on the signed-in device and approve the request. The other device signs in without a keyboard.

## Voice

Dictate an idea and Todos turns it into a todo, which an agent then runs on your machines. This is what makes filing work from a phone practical — the gap between having the thought and having it queued is a few seconds.

## What is web-only

A few things need a browser, and the app says so where it applies:

- Adding a GitHub account or organization — its authorization returns to a browser
- Creating skills, including importing a folder from disk
- Billing: upgrading, changing payment details, cancelling

Everything else — the board, conversations, plans, diffs, reviews, machines, agents — works the same on both.

## Where next

- [Inbox and notifications](/docs/inbox) — why the Home Screen step matters.
- [Conversations](/docs/conversation) — voice, images, steering.
- [Install](/docs/install) — the rest of the setup.

<!-- source: https://todos.dev/docs/teams -->

# Teams

A team is the unit everything belongs to. Members, agents, machines, projects, model providers, secrets, and skills are all team-scoped, and billing is per team rather than per seat.

One person can belong to several teams and switch between them. Each team has its own Chief, its own charter, and its own view of the work.

## Members

Open the team page and go to **Members**. The tab shows you and the agents on the team.

**Create agent** adds an agent. See [Agents](/docs/agents).

The person who creates the team is its captain. Team admins configure providers, secrets, machines, and the switches on each agent; members can see those settings without changing them.

Removing an agent is done from the same tab. Inviting other people to a team is not available yet.

## Team settings

The General tab carries the team's name, id, creation date, storage in use, and current plan, along with the avatar style used for agents.

If the team has no model provider configured, this page says so — agents on it have nothing to run on until one is added. See [Model providers](/docs/providers).

## Machines

**Resources → Machines** (also the Machines tab in team settings) lists every enrolled machine with its state and badges: remote shell, builds off, update available. **Add machine** shows the enrollment commands.

See [Machines](/docs/machines).

## Plans

Your plan sets capacity for agents, machines, parallel builds, and storage. Every feature is available on every plan; paid tiers buy capacity, not features.

Billing is handled in the web app. See [pricing](/pricing) for the numbers.

## Where next

- [Agents](/docs/agents) — who does the work on the team.
- [Permissions](/docs/permissions) — what an admin may do that a member may not.
- [Projects](/docs/projects) — what the team's work is organised into.

---

<!-- source: https://todos.dev/docs/projects -->

# Projects

A project is a git repository plus the work happening in it. Todos belong to projects; agents and machines belong to the team and move freely between them.

A project cannot run anything until a repository is connected.

## Connect a repository

Open the project and click **Connect repository**, or pick a repository while creating it. Two options:

**A GitHub repository.** Search your connected accounts and organizations, pick a repository and a base branch. **Add GitHub account or organization** connects a new one; that authorization returns to a browser, so it happens in the web app. See [GitHub](/docs/github).

**A new repository on Todos.** No GitHub account needed. Todos creates a fresh repository on its own hosting, with a README on a `main` base branch. See [Repos on Todos](/docs/platform-git).

Once connected, a project's repository cannot be changed. Connecting one takes a team admin.

## Base branch

The base branch is what agents branch from and merge back into. It is shown in the project's settings, with the default one tagged.

If the branch disappears from the remote, settings flags it and asks you to choose another.

## Project settings

| | |
|---|---|
| Name | Renameable at any time |
| Repo | The connected repository, shown read-only |
| Base branch | Changeable |
| Description | Optional context, shown to agents |
| Clone locally | The exact `git clone` command, with a copy button |

Cloning a Todos-hosted repository needs an API key with git access. Read allows clone, fetch, and pull; write allows push. See [API keys](/docs/api-keys).

## Files

The **Files** page (the folder icon on the project page) browses the repository on any branch — the picker labels each todo's branch with its number and title. Single files download from there; on a phone the download hands off to the share sheet. The page's URL carries the branch and the open file (`ref`, `path`), so any view can be shared as a link.

Uploading a file into the open directory, or deleting one from the file pane, lands as a commit on that branch's head — you are the commit's author. Uploads cap at 50MB. Both actions hide while viewing a commit snapshot, which has no branch head to move.

## Tags

Tags group todos within a project. Create one from a todo's tag field, filter the board by it, and manage the set from the Tags page — where each tag shows how many todos carry it, and removing one takes it off every todo at once.

## Deleting a project

Deleting a project permanently deletes all of its todos and builds. It cannot be undone.

## Where next

- [Todos](/docs/todos) — the work inside a project.
- [GitHub](/docs/github) — connecting accounts, branches, pull requests.
- [Repos on Todos](/docs/platform-git) — projects with no GitHub at all.

---

<!-- source: https://todos.dev/docs/platform-git -->

# Repos on Todos

Every project needs a git repository, but it does not have to be hosted on GitHub. When you create a project you can pick **Create a new repository on Todos** instead of connecting a GitHub account.

Todos creates a fresh repository on its own git hosting, and your agents clone, build, and merge against it exactly as they would a GitHub repo. No GitHub account, no app install, no browser round-trip.

## Create one

Click **New project**, open the repository picker, choose **Create a new repository on Todos**, name the project, and create it.

The repository starts with a single commit — a README — on a `main` base branch. Agents then work from this base. Their work lands on the project like any other, and you review it in the conversation with the built-in diff viewer.

## How merging works

Todos-hosted repositories have no pull requests. Review takes place in the usual location: the conversation, with the diff and [AI review](/docs/ai-review).

When you complete the todo with merge selected, an agent turn reconciles the work with the base branch, resolving any conflicts, and the base branch is then fast-forwarded directly. The branch panel shows "Merged into the base branch" once it lands.

Because there is no PR object, a few GitHub-specific tools are absent on these projects: `merge_branch`, `create_tag`, and the GitHub Actions tools. Agents are informed of this when relevant.

## Differences from a GitHub project

| | Hosted on Todos |
|---|---|
| Repository page | None. The repository is reachable by your agents and shown through the product — diffs, file viewer — without a public web UI |
| Pull requests | None. Direct fast-forward as described above |
| CI | No GitHub Actions equivalent yet |
| Local git access | Per API key, off by default |

## Clone and push locally

Git access is a per-key setting, off by default. Create a key under [**API keys**](/docs/api-keys), turn on **Git access**, and pick its scope: read covers clone, fetch, and pull; write covers push and always includes read.

```bash
git clone https://git.todos.dev/<team>/<repo>.git
```

The exact command for a project is shown in its settings, with a copy button. When git asks for credentials, use any username and the key as the password. Access is limited to members of the project's team; a key without git access is refused.

If the machine you want the code on is one that runs the project's builds, there is an even simpler path: ask an agent in a task to clone the code into a folder you name — it copies from its own working tree with plain git, without requiring a key.

A write-scoped key can push to any branch, including the base branch, which makes it the way to import existing work:

```bash
git remote add todos https://git.todos.dev/<team>/<repo>.git
git push todos main
```

## Limits

A hosted repository can grow to 2 GB. Pushes that would exceed the limit are rejected with a clear error.

## Where next

- [Projects](/docs/projects) — connecting a repository, base branches, tags.
- [GitHub](/docs/github) — the other kind of project.
- [API keys](/docs/api-keys) — the git scopes cloning needs.

---

<!-- source: https://todos.dev/docs/machines -->

# Machines

A machine is where runs happen. Machines claim runs; agents do not own them. When a todo starts, it goes to whichever machine is free and taking builds — unless you pin the run to one.

There are two kinds. Your own machines are computers you enroll by running `tds start`, and they are what this page is about. A [platform machine](/docs/platform-machines) is one Todos runs for you — asleep while idle, awake as soon as there is work — and comes with Pro.

Until at least one machine is available, nothing runs.

## Enroll one

```bash
npm install -g @todos-dev/cli@latest
tds start
```

The first run opens a browser to authorize a team. On a headless server, use an API key instead:

```bash
tds start --api-key <key> --team <team-id>
```

New machines appear under **Resources → Machines**. See [CLI](/docs/cli) for every flag.

## Per-machine switches

Each machine's page carries two independent switches. The running daemon picks changes up within a few seconds — no restart needed.

| Switch | Effect |
|---|---|
| Builds | Claims build, plan, and review tasks and runs the agent |
| Remote shell | Lets granted agents run commands on this machine. See [Remote shell](/docs/remote-shell) |

Turning builds off leaves the machine enrolled and available for shell while it takes no new work.

## Concurrency

Each machine has its own limit on how many runs it takes at once, a whole number of 1 or more. It sits alongside the team's parallel-build cap: a run needs room under both.

## Pin work to one machine

By default the platform picks. To name a machine instead, change **Machine** from **Automatic** to it:

| Where | What it covers |
|---|---|
| Start build panel | That one build. Fixed when the build is created, and every turn of it runs there |
| Schedule dialog | Every build that rule fires from then on |
| Chief settings | Where the chief's own conversation runs; can be changed at any time |

The picker marks each machine **online**, **offline**, or — for a platform machine — **asleep**. A sleeping machine wakes when the work starts; no action is needed.

You can also tell the chief "run this on \<machine\>". It pins only when you name a machine, and leaves everything else to automatic selection.

**A pin never falls back.** That machine is the only machine, and the platform will not substitute another when it cannot take the work:

| Situation | What happens |
|---|---|
| Your own machine is offline | The turn fails outright, and says why in the thread |
| A platform machine is asleep | It wakes and the run proceeds |
| Removed from the team, or builds turned off | Refused with the reason; pick another machine or go back to automatic |
| CLI too old, or too old for this project's git host | Same, and upgrading that machine's CLI clears it |

Schedules deserve care here. A rule set to **Automatic** skips a cycle when nothing is online and runs normally once a machine returns. A pinned rule does not skip — it fires, fails on the spot, and spends a build slot doing so, every cycle. Pin a recurring rule to something that stays up, or leave it automatic.

## Choosing a machine

Under automatic selection an offline machine is simply not considered, so closing your laptop does not block anyone else's work. Pinning changes that: the pinned machine's uptime becomes the work's uptime.

So pin to something that is up anyway — a [platform machine](/docs/platform-machines), or a cloud box that keeps `tds start` running. A laptop is a good fit for automatic selection and a poor one for schedules and long-standing pins.

The two always-on options differ in one place: a platform machine cannot be a remote shell target and a cloud box can. If you want both, use the cloud box.

## Running commands on the machine

To read a log, run a command, restart a service, or reach the dev server running on your own box, use remote shell — an agent running commands there.

Two switches have to be on: **Remote shell** on this machine, and the grant on the agent itself. The quickest route is to ask the chief — "let the frontend agent run commands on my laptop" — and it turns on both ends.

The shell is persistent and stateful: working directory, environment variables and background processes survive between calls for as long as the machine stays connected. A dev server started in one call is still running in the next.

A platform machine cannot do this — it does not run the tunnel this needs. Enroll a machine of your own for it. Full details in [Remote shell](/docs/remote-shell).

## The machine page

Beyond the switches, a machine's page shows its running tasks and its CLI version.

When the machine is stopped, the page says so and prints the commands to start it. When its CLI is behind, an **update available** badge appears with the upgrade and restart commands:

```bash
npm install -g @todos-dev/cli@latest
tds restart
```

An out-of-date CLI is not cosmetic. Machines below a minimum version cannot receive model credentials configured on the website, and older ones cannot receive team secrets.

## Offline and removal

A machine that stops responding for over 10 minutes has its in-flight run settled as failed rather than left hanging. One that comes back within those 10 minutes resumes on its own with nothing lost.

A sleeping platform machine is not offline: it sleeps because there is nothing to do, and dispatching work wakes it.

**Remove machine** deauthorizes it; it must enroll again to come back. Removing a machine mid-run fails that run, which can then be run again on another machine.

`tds logout` is the local counterpart: it clears the registration on the machine but does not remove it from the team.

## Limits

Your plan sets how many machines a team may enroll and how many builds may run at once; a platform machine counts against the same number. Enrolling past the cap fails with a clear error rather than queueing. See [pricing](/pricing) for the numbers.

## Where next

- [Platform machines](/docs/platform-machines) — the path that needs no machine of your own.
- [CLI](/docs/cli) — commands, flags, files on disk.
- [Remote shell](/docs/remote-shell) — letting an agent run commands here.
- [Troubleshooting](/docs/troubleshooting) — machine-related run errors.

---

<!-- source: https://todos.dev/docs/platform-machines -->

# Platform machines

A platform machine is one Todos runs for you: no computer of your own to keep on, nothing to install. It sleeps while idle, wakes on its own when work is queued, and draws credits only while awake. In every other respect it is [a machine](/docs/machines) like any other — it claims tasks, runs agents, and pushes branches.

## Get one

Platform machines come with Pro, one per team. After upgrading, onboarding creates the team's machine for you, so there is usually nothing to add by hand.

To add one yourself: **Resources → Machines** → **Add a platform machine**. This is a team-admin action. Free has no such option — enroll a machine of your own with `tds start` instead.

## Sizes and cost

A platform machine is a container running on Cloudflare Sandboxes, and the three sizes are its instance configurations. Size is the one dial a team turns day to day.

| Size | vCPU | Memory | Disk | Default concurrency | Credits per awake hour | 35,000 credits buys |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Small (default) | 1 | 6 GiB | 12 GB | 3 | 340 | 102 hours |
| Medium | 2 | 8 GiB | 16 GB | 5 | 490 | 71 hours |
| Large | 4 | 12 GiB | 20 GB | 8 | 785 | 44 hours |

Sleeping costs nothing at any size — the bill follows awake time and nothing else. Machine time and platform-paid inference draw on the same monthly credit pool; see [pricing](/pricing) for the numbers.

Credits are denominated at what the platform actually pays: machine time and inference alike are billed at cost with no platform markup. Only a payment processing fee is added when topping up.

Sizes go up only. Small is a floor: anything smaller cannot hold the image plus a repo clone plus an install of its dependencies.

## Sleeping and waking

After 10 idle minutes the machine sleeps. From then on, queued work wakes it on its own — a cold start is usually seconds, and it shows in the build as a **Waking machine** stage.

A machine stays awake for as long as a task runs on it; nothing is cut off by the idle timer. When the task ends, the workspace is backed up and the clock starts over.

The machine page says whether it is **awake** or **asleep**, and while awake it estimates how many minutes until it sleeps.

Asleep is not a fault and needs no action. Dispatching work is how you wake it.

## Resizing

Pick a new size under **Machine size** on the machine page. It can take effect two ways:

| Way | When | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Save, applies on next wake | Next wake | Free, interrupts nothing |
| Restart now to switch | About a minute | Restarts immediately; refused while a build is running |

Neither loses the workspace: it is saved before the switch and restored after.

## Disk and workspace

A platform machine's container disk is ephemeral — destroyed on every sleep, restored from a backup on the next wake. So it is not a place to keep files: an agent's output belongs on the todo's branch, as covered in [plans and diffs](/docs/plans-and-diffs).

A failed backup loses no committed work. The worst case is a cold start from an empty disk on the next wake, which costs time re-cloning.

## What it cannot do

| Limit | Detail |
|---|---|
| Not a remote-shell target | [Remote shell](/docs/remote-shell) rides the sync tunnel, which platform machines run without. Enroll a machine of your own when you need it |
| One on Pro | For more capacity, resize it, or enroll your own machine with `tds start` |
| Stops waking when credits run out | Your own machines and your own API keys are unaffected — there is always a path that costs nothing |
| Removal destroys it | Removing a platform machine destroys its sandbox and its saved workspace disk. A team's last one cannot be removed while its plan includes one |

A self-hosted Todos server with no sandbox backend configured never shows the platform-machine option at all.

## Where next

- [Machines](/docs/machines) — enrolling your own, its switches, offline behavior.
- [Pricing](/pricing) — credits, plan allowances, top-ups.
- [Troubleshooting](/docs/troubleshooting) — machine-related run errors.

---

<!-- source: https://todos.dev/docs/providers -->

# Model providers

Agents run on AI models, and models need credentials. Providers are configured once for the whole team, on this website: **Resources → Providers**.

Keys are stored encrypted on the server. A machine receives exactly the credential a task needs, at the moment the task starts, and holds it in memory only. Change or remove a key and the next task runs with the new configuration.

Managing providers needs team admin permission. Members can see what is configured.

## Add a provider

Pick what you have on the **Add provider** screen.

**An API key from a model vendor.** Choose the vendor — OpenAI, DeepSeek, Google, xAI, OpenRouter, and more — paste the key, save. The key is verified with one real model request first, so a bad paste fails here rather than in your next task. A merely rate-limited account still saves; only a rejected key is refused. Verification can be skipped when the vendor is unreachable from our servers.

**A subscription you already pay for.** ChatGPT/Codex and GitHub Copilot have no API keys at all. xAI takes either, so picking it asks which you want. The page shows a short code and a link; you sign in at the vendor, and the connection lands once we have proved it can run a model.

A provider holds one credential at a time, so signing in to xAI replaces an xAI API key the team already had. If a subscription login expires later, the provider shows a reconnect prompt.

**A custom OpenAI-compatible endpoint.** Enter the base URL, usually ending in `/v1`, pick the protocol it speaks, and add its models. The page asks the endpoint for its model list where possible; otherwise enter model ids by hand. A key is optional, for gateways that need none.

## What machines see

Machines never store provider credentials. When a machine picks up a task, the server hands it the one credential and model definition that task uses, over the same authenticated channel the task arrives on. The credential lives in memory for that task and is fetched fresh for the next one.

This is why edits take effect immediately: no cache to expire, no sync to wait for, no per-machine setup. Every machine on the team can run every model in the catalog.

## The model picker

An agent's model picker lists exactly what the team's providers offer. Add a provider and its models appear within seconds. Remove one and its models leave the picker; tasks still assigned to them fail with a pointer back to this page.

The catalog knows what a provider offers in general, not what your account is entitled to, and vendors retire models without notice. If a task reports that the vendor does not have a model, assign one that still exists.

## Key storage

Keys are encrypted at rest with a dedicated master key, and are never returned by any page or API after saving — editing a provider always starts from a blank key field. They are decrypted only at the moment a task is dispatched to your own machine.

Subscription refreshes are performed by the server alone. Two machines refreshing the same login independently used to invalidate one another.

## Older CLIs

Machines running `tds` older than 0.1.35 keep reading keys from their own disk and never see anything configured here. On each machine run `npm install -g @todos-dev/cli@latest` and `tds restart`.

## Where next

- [Agents](/docs/agents) — choosing a model and thinking level per agent.
- [Secrets](/docs/secrets) — credentials for the work itself, not for the model.
- [Troubleshooting](/docs/troubleshooting) — what each provider error means.

---

<!-- source: https://todos.dev/docs/mcp-servers -->

# MCP servers

Team MCP servers are the outside tools your agents reach for while working — a ticket tracker, a browser, an internal API. You register a server once for the team, grant it to the agents that need it, and its tools appear alongside their built-in ones.

This is the outbound direction. [MCP](/docs/mcp) is the other one: there, Todos is the server and your editor connects in to read the board. The two are unrelated — a client connecting in does not need anything on this page.

Agents reach MCP tools only on machines running tds CLI v0.1.45 or later. Older machines ignore the grant silently; run `npm install -g @todos-dev/cli@latest`, then `tds restart`.

## Add a server

Open **Resources → MCP** and click **Add MCP server**. Managing servers needs team admin permission; members can see what is registered.

| Field | |
|---|---|
| Type | Remote (HTTP) or local command (stdio) — see below |
| Name | What people see in lists, such as `Linear` |
| Identifier | Lowercase slug, unique per team. Becomes the tool-name prefix `mcp__<slug>__<tool>`, and cannot be changed later |

A team can register up to 20 servers.

The type and identifier are fixed once saved. To change either, delete the server and add it again — grants do not survive that, so re-grant it to the agents that had it.

## Remote or local

**Remote (HTTP)** connects to a hosted MCP endpoint by URL. Authentication goes in optional request headers.

**Local command (stdio)** runs a command on whichever machine picks up the task. Arguments are one whitespace-separated line — quoted arguments with spaces are not supported. Anything the process needs in its environment goes in the env vars.

Prefer remote when the tool offers it: a local command has to be installed on every machine that might run the work, and a machine missing it simply cannot use the tool.

## Credentials

Headers and env vars are write-only, like [secrets](/docs/secrets). They are encrypted at rest and never returned by any read route.

Editing a server shows the names of the stored keys with blank value fields. Type a new value to overwrite that key, leave it blank to keep what is stored. New rows add a key, or overwrite one of the same name. Untouched keys survive a save; to remove a key entirely, delete the server and add it back.

Values are decrypted only when a machine claims the step, and ride that one response. They are never queued, never logged, and never written to the executor's disk.

## Grant a server to an agent

Registering a server does not hand it to anyone. On the agent's page, add the server to its **MCP servers** list. Each agent can hold up to 10.

Grants are per agent, not per task, and per server rather than all-or-nothing — an agent gets exactly the servers you pick. Changes take effect from that agent's next turn.

## Removing a server

Deleting takes the tools away from every agent that had it, from their next turn onward. Work already running finishes with what it claimed.

An agent granted a server that no longer exists is not an error — the missing grant is dropped when the step is assembled, and the agent runs without those tools.

## Where next

- [Agents](/docs/agents) — where a grant is made, next to skills and permissions.
- [Secrets](/docs/secrets) — credentials for the agent's own shell, stored the same way.
- [MCP](/docs/mcp) — the inbound direction: connecting your editor to Todos.

---

<!-- source: https://todos.dev/docs/secrets -->

# Secrets

Team secrets are named credentials — API keys, tokens, service passwords — that your agents can use while working. You save a secret once, grant it to the agents that need it, and it appears as an environment variable in every shell command those agents run.

Never paste a real credential into a conversation. Chat messages are stored with the conversation forever; secrets have their own path.

## Add a secret

Open **Resources → Secrets** and click **Add secret**. Managing secrets needs team admin permission; members can see the names.

| Field | |
|---|---|
| Name | The environment variable the agent will see, such as `STRIPE_API_KEY` |
| Description | Optional but recommended — agents read it to know what the variable is for |
| Value | Pasted once, then never shown again |

Secrets are write-only. After saving, nobody can view the value again, including admins. You can overwrite it or delete it, and that is all — which is what you want from credential storage. Keep the original in your own password manager.

## Grant a secret to an agent

Secrets do not flow to every agent automatically. On the agent's page, turn on **Team secrets**. From that agent's next turn, every secret in the team's library is available in its shell.

Chief can flip this switch too when you ask — it grants secrets the same way it grants tools and skills, acting as you, so you need to be a team admin. It never does so on its own initiative.

Secrets are granted per agent, not per task. To scope a credential tightly, grant it to a dedicated agent and give that agent only the work that needs it.

## What the agent sees

The agent is told which variables exist — names and descriptions only — so it knows `$STRIPE_API_KEY` is there to use.

Values are injected directly into the shell process. They are not in the prompt, not in the conversation, and not in the stored transcript.

Agents are instructed not to print secret values, but a shell command that echoes one would still show it in the tool output. Grant secrets to agents you would trust with the underlying credential.

## When a variable is missing

Check three things: the secret exists on the Secrets page, the agent's **Team secrets** switch is on, and the machine's CLI is current. Changes take effect from the next turn.

A task that fails with "runs a tds CLI without team-secrets support" is on a machine with an older CLI. Run `npm install -g @todos-dev/cli@latest`, then `tds restart`, and retry.

## Where next

- [Permissions](/docs/permissions) — every per-agent switch in one table.
- [Model providers](/docs/providers) — credentials for models, stored separately.
- [Remote shell](/docs/remote-shell) — the other switch only a human can grant.

---

<!-- source: https://todos.dev/docs/permissions -->

# Permissions

Authorization in Todos is spread across four places: what an agent may do, what a machine allows, what a person's role permits, and what an API key carries. This page collects all of it.

## Agent tools

Every agent starts able to read and edit files, run commands inside its own build, read the team's todos, ask you a question, and notify you. Those need no grant.

These are per-agent switches, off until turned on, on the agent's page under **Tools**:

| Tool | What it allows | Who may grant it |
|---|---|---|
| Push branch | Pushing the build branch to the remote | Team admin, or Chief |
| Merge branch | Merging into the base branch | Team admin, or Chief |
| Create tag | Tagging a release | Team admin, or Chief |
| Create skill | Writing a new skill into the team library | Team admin, or Chief |
| Update skill | Editing an existing skill | Team admin, or Chief |
| Remote shell | Running commands on your machines | Team admin, or Chief |
| Team secrets | Reading the team's secrets as environment variables | Team admin, or Chief |

Every grant is yours or Chief's to give. Chief acts as you, so you need to be a team admin, and it only grants on your explicit request — it never hands out shell access or credentials on its own initiative.

Grants take effect from the agent's next turn.

## Machine switches

An agent's grant is not enough on its own. Each machine has its own consent, on its page:

| Switch | Effect when off |
|---|---|
| Builds | The machine claims no new runs |
| Remote shell | No agent reaches this machine, whatever grants it carries |

Remote shell needs the agent's grant **and** the machine's switch. To scope an agent that already has `remote_shell`, turn shell access off on the machines it should not reach — the grant itself is team-wide.

## People

| | Admin | Member |
|---|---|---|
| Read the board, file todos, confirm and review | Yes | Yes |
| Configure model providers | Yes | Read-only |
| Add, edit, delete secrets | Yes | Names only |
| Flip an agent's tool switches | Yes | Read-only |
| Flip a machine's switches, remove machines | Yes | Read-only |
| Connect a repository to a project | Yes | No |
| Remove agents | Yes | No |

Chief acts as you. It can only do what you could do, so an admin-only action asked of Chief by a member fails the same way.

Schedule rules are the exception that follows ownership rather than role: only a todo's owner may add, edit, or remove them.

## API keys

Keys are per person and act as their owner, with two independent kinds of access, both off by default: MCP tools, in read and write groups, and git access scoped read or write. See [API keys](/docs/api-keys).

A key never exceeds its owner's own permissions.

## Where next

- [Agents](/docs/agents) — where the tool switches live.
- [Secrets](/docs/secrets) — the credentials behind one of them.
- [Remote shell](/docs/remote-shell) — the two-switch grant in detail.
- [Teams](/docs/teams) — roles and membership.

---

<!-- source: https://todos.dev/docs/remote-shell -->

# Remote shell

An agent works inside a sandboxed build. It cannot reach your local files, your dev servers, or your device. Remote shell gives it a controlled path onto a machine you own.

Two switches have to be on: **Remote shell** on the machine, and **Remote shell** on the agent. From its next turn the agent sees a `remote_shell` tool alongside `bash`.

The quickest route is to ask Chief — "let the frontend fixer run commands on my laptop" — and it flips both, then tells you what now reaches what.

## Enable it on the machine

Once the machine is online, open it from **Resources → Machines** and turn on **Remote shell**.

This is machine-level consent: without it no agent reaches this machine, whatever grants it carries. It takes a team admin. Members can see the setting but not change it.

Only a machine you run yourself can be a target. A platform machine runs without the tunnel remote shell rides, so the switch cannot be turned on there — on a team whose only machine is the platform one, enroll a computer of your own first.

The machines list shows a remote shell badge next to every machine that has it enabled.

## Grant it to an agent

Open the team page, go to **Members**, click the agent, and under **Tools** turn on **Remote shell**.

The grant takes effect from the agent's next turn. It is agent-wide: an agent with `remote_shell` reaches every machine in the team that has shell access enabled. To narrow that, disable shell access on machines the agent should not reach.

Chief can set up both halves when you ask, acting as you, so it needs you to be a team admin. It will not hand out remote shell on its own initiative.

## What the shell behaves like

The shell is persistent and stateful. The working directory, environment variables, and background processes survive between calls, as long as the machine stays online. If the connection drops the shell dies, and the next call opens a fresh one with a visible reconnect note.

Commands start in the machine's home directory, and the agent can navigate anywhere your user account can reach. Grant remote shell only to agents you trust with the machine's filesystem.

The agent picks a target machine by name. With one shell-enabled machine it uses that one; with several it asks you.

The tool returns output once the shell goes quiet, about a second of idle time, or after a timeout. For long-running commands the agent polls with empty input to read more. It can send `Ctrl-C` to interrupt.

Dev servers and other long-running processes are fine. They survive between calls while the shell stays connected.

## When the tool is missing

Both switches must be on: the agent's grant, and shell access on at least one machine. Chief can read both and fix either.
