If the agent reports no machine available, the machine may be offline — check `tds status` — its shell switch may be off, or its CLI may be too old.

The tunnel is part of the CLI and redials itself: there is no separate daemon, sidecar, or install script. A machine whose tunnel will not come up is failing at its own network path to the control plane, and `tds logs` on that machine shows why.

## Where next

- [Permissions](/docs/permissions) — every switch, and who may flip it.
- [Machines](/docs/machines) — the per-machine switches.

---

<!-- source: https://todos.dev/docs/cli -->

# CLI

`tds` is the command line tool that brings a machine online. It is the only thing you install locally; the board, conversations, and reviews all live in the browser or the app.

Install it on every computer that should run builds. Node.js 22.19 or newer is required:

```bash
npm install -g @todos-dev/cli@latest
```

## Commands

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `tds start` | Bring this machine online in the background, enrolling it if needed |
| `tds stop` | Stop the background machine |
| `tds restart` | Stop and start again, taking the same options as `start` |
| `tds logs` | Print the background machine's log |
| `tds status` | Show this machine's registration and current state |
| `tds logout` | Forget this machine's local registration |
| `tds version` | Print the installed CLI version |

`tds --help` lists them. `tds <command> --help` prints one command's usage.

## tds start

By default this detaches and runs in the background, supervised so it survives a crash. On first run — when there is no local registration — it enrolls the machine into a team.

With no flags, it opens a browser to sign in and pick the team to authorize. With `--api-key`, it enrolls non-interactively, which is what a headless server or a CI runner needs.

| Option | Effect |
|---|---|
| `--foreground`, `-f` | Run attached in this terminal, unsupervised. Use it when pm2, systemd, or a container already supervises `tds` |
| `--api-key <key>` | Enroll with an API key. Requires `--team`, and overwrites an existing registration to switch team or account |
| `--team <id>` | Team to join, used with `--api-key` |
| `--name <name>` | Machine display name. Defaults to the hostname |
| `--server <url>` | Override the server URL |
| `--workspaces-dir <dir>` | Root for cloned repos and worktrees. Defaults to `~/.tds/workspaces` |

`--workspaces-dir` is persisted across restarts, which makes it the way to keep heavy checkouts on an external drive. The parent directory must already exist: if the drive is unmounted, `tds` refuses to start rather than cloning onto the boot disk. Existing clones are not moved when the directory changes.

Agent shell access is managed from the machine's page in the app. The running daemon picks the change up within a few seconds — no restart needed.

## tds logs

```bash
tds logs      # print ~/.tds/daemon.log
tds logs -f   # follow it, like tail -f
```

The log rotates past 10 MB.

## tds stop and tds logout

`tds stop` sends SIGTERM so in-flight tasks shut down cleanly, and only SIGKILLs if the process does not exit in time.

`tds logout` stops the daemon and clears the local registration, so the next `tds start` enrolls again. It is local only — it does not remove the machine from the team. An admin does that on the machine's page.

## Environment variables

| Variable | Effect |
|---|---|
| `TDS_SERVER` | Default server URL |
| `TDS_API_KEY` | API key for non-interactive enroll |
| `TDS_TEAM` | Team for `--api-key` enroll |
| `TDS_WORKSPACES_DIR` | One-shot override of the workspaces root, not persisted |

Prefer `tds start --workspaces-dir` over `TDS_WORKSPACES_DIR`: the flag is remembered, the variable is not.

`HTTP_PROXY` and `HTTPS_PROXY` are honoured, as is the macOS system proxy.

## Files on disk

| Path | Contents |
|---|---|
| `~/.tds/machine.json` | This machine's registration. Mode `600` |
| `~/.tds/device.json` | Hardware fingerprint. Kept by `tds logout` so re-enrolling reuses the same machine |
| `~/.tds/daemon.log` | Background daemon log |
| `~/.tds/workspaces/` | Cloned repositories and worktrees, unless `--workspaces-dir` moved them |

## tds provider

Model providers moved to the website. The command remains only to point you there: configure them under **Resources → Providers**, per team. Machines receive credentials with each task, so there is nothing to set up locally. See [Model providers](/docs/providers).

## Where next

- [Machines](/docs/machines) — concurrency, per-machine switches, offline behaviour.
- [API keys](/docs/api-keys) — creating the key `--api-key` needs.
- [Troubleshooting](/docs/troubleshooting) — what a failed run's error means.

---

<!-- source: https://todos.dev/docs/mcp -->

# MCP

Todos includes a remote MCP server. Once connected, clients such as Claude Code, Cursor, and VS Code can read your board, create and refine todos, inspect build conversations, run or cancel builds, and request independent reviews.

Two items are required: the server URL and an API key with MCP access enabled.

## Create an API key

Open [**API keys**](/docs/api-keys) from your avatar menu, click **New key**, and turn on **MCP access**.

Select only the tools this client needs. A client that only inspects work needs only read tools.

Create the key and copy the value beginning with `tds_` immediately — the plaintext is shown once.

Assign each client its own key. This makes permissions easier to narrow, and revoking one client does not disturb the others.

## Connect a client

The server URL is shown under **MCP** in the sidebar. For todos.dev:

```text
https://todos.dev/api/mcp
```

Add this to the client's configuration, replacing `tds_your_key` with your key:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "todos": {
      "url": "https://todos.dev/api/mcp",
      "headers": {
        "Authorization": "Bearer tds_your_key"
      }
    }
  }
}
```

Clients store MCP configuration in different places, but the server fields are identical: a remote URL plus an `Authorization: Bearer <key>` header. VS Code uses a `servers` key instead of `mcpServers`; `url` and `headers` are unchanged.

After saving, reload the client or its MCP server list. A successful connection exposes only the tools that key allows.

## What a client can do

| Group | Capabilities |
|---|---|
| Read the workspace | List projects, list todos across them, read a todo in full, see available agents, machines, and skills, read attachments |
| Read the repo | Read GitHub issues (the spec behind "work on this issue"), pull requests with merge state, and CI workflow runs — read-only, GitHub-backed projects only |
| Read progress | Inspect the complete conversation from a todo's latest build — including any turn still streaming — to take over work or diagnose a failure |
| Organize work | Create todos, update titles, specs, and tags |
| Run work | Start or cancel builds, ask another agent for an independent review |
| Manage lifecycle | Mark todos done, close them, reopen them |

MCP calls act as the key's owner and can reach projects in that user's teams. The key's tool selection limits every call: a client cannot invoke a tool it was not granted.

Grant the least access the client needs. Read tools alone cover search, summaries, and status reports. Add create and update to capture backlog items. Add build, cancel, and review to dispatch agents. Grant done, close, and reopen only when the client genuinely maintains board state.

Changes to a key's tool selection apply to subsequent requests. Removing every MCP tool disables MCP for that key, and does not affect machines that hold their own machine token.

## Errors

| Symptom | Cause |
|---|---|
| 401 Unauthorized | Header is not `Authorization: Bearer tds_...`, the key has stray whitespace, the key was revoked, or the client cannot send custom headers |
| 403, no MCP access | The key has no MCP tools selected. Enable MCP access and select at least one |
| Connects, but a tool is missing | The client sees only what its key allows. Update the selection, then reconnect |
| The client asks for OAuth | Todos MCP uses a Bearer API key and offers no OAuth. Use a client that lets you set a header |

Do not include an MCP key in a todo conversation. Keep it in the client's configuration or a credential store, and out of git.

## Where next

- [API keys](/docs/api-keys) — scopes, rotation, revocation.
- [Permissions](/docs/permissions) — how MCP scopes sit beside the other switches.
- [MCP servers](/docs/mcp-servers) — the opposite direction: giving your agents outside tools.

---

<!-- source: https://todos.dev/docs/api-keys -->

# API keys

An API key authenticates something that is not a browser: a machine enrolling without a sign-in, an MCP client, or a local `git clone`.

Keys are per person, not per team, and act as their owner. Create them from **API keys** in your avatar menu.

## Create a key

Click **New key**, name it, and pick its access. The plaintext value begins with `tds_` and is shown once — copy it immediately.

Give each consumer its own key. Narrowing or revoking one then leaves the others alone.

## Access

A key carries two independent kinds of access, both off by default.

**MCP access** selects which MCP tools the key may call, in read and write groups. A client that only inspects work needs read tools alone. Removing every MCP tool disables MCP for that key. See [MCP](/docs/mcp).

**Git access** has two scopes:

| Scope | Covers |
|---|---|
| Read | clone, fetch, pull |
| Write | push. Always includes read |

Git access applies to repositories hosted on Todos, and is limited to teams the key's owner belongs to. See [Repos on Todos](/docs/platform-git).

## Enrolling a machine

A headless server has no browser to sign in with, so it enrolls with a key instead:

```bash
tds start --api-key <key> --team <team-id>
```

This needs no MCP or git access — enrollment is its own path. See [CLI](/docs/cli).

## Revoking

**Revoke** invalidates a key immediately for MCP and git.

Machines already enrolled keep running: enrollment exchanges the key for the machine's own token, so revoking the key does not take a machine offline. Remove the machine from **Resources → Machines** to do that.

## Handling

Do not paste a key into a todo conversation — messages are stored with the conversation permanently. Keep keys out of git and out of client configs that sync publicly.

Credentials your agents need for their work belong in [Secrets](/docs/secrets), not in an API key.

## Where next

- [MCP](/docs/mcp) — connecting an outside client.
- [Repos on Todos](/docs/platform-git) — what git access unlocks.
- [Permissions](/docs/permissions) — every switch in one table.

---

<!-- source: https://todos.dev/docs/github -->

# GitHub

A project can be connected to a GitHub repository, and agents then branch, push, and open pull requests against it exactly as a person would.

If you would rather not involve GitHub at all, a project can use a repository hosted on Todos instead. See [Repos on Todos](/docs/platform-git).

## Connect an account

Connecting a repository starts from the project's repository picker. **Add GitHub account or organization** asks for the username or organization to connect, checks it exists and is available, and sends you to GitHub to install the app.

This authorization returns to a browser, so it is done in the web app rather than on a phone.

An account or organization can belong to one Todos team at a time, so connecting one that is already held is refused. There are two ways forward:

- **A team you administer holds it**: the message offers a disconnect button and retries for you afterwards. You can also disconnect it under that team's **Settings → GitHub accounts**.
- **Someone else's team holds it**: uninstall the Todos app on GitHub — from [your app settings](https://github.com/settings/installations) for a personal account, or the organization's Installed GitHub Apps — then come back and retry.

Disconnecting uninstalls the Todos app from that GitHub account, so projects in the former team that use it can no longer push, pull, or open pull requests.

## Connect a repository

Once an account is connected, search its repositories, pick one, and choose the base branch. Private repositories are marked as such.

A long list is truncated with a note; search narrows it.

Once connected, a project's repository cannot be changed.

## Branches and pull requests

Each build works on its own branch off the base branch.

**Push branch**, **Merge branch**, and **Create tag** are per-agent switches, off by default. An agent without them works in its checkout without publishing anything. See [Permissions](/docs/permissions).

At Review, the branch icon in the todo header opens **Branch and pull request**, which shows the build branch and its state:

| State | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Changes are ready to submit | **Submit** opens a pull request |
| A pull request is available | **View PR** opens it on GitHub |
| Merged into the base branch | Already landed |
| Changes are on the branch | Submittable once the todo reaches Review |
| No branch changes yet | Nothing produced so far |

Opening a pull request is separate from completing the todo. **Done** completes it, optionally merging into the default branch.

## Revoked authorization

If the GitHub App is uninstalled or its access is revoked, runs fail with an authentication error naming the repository. Re-authorize the account, then run the todo again — nothing is lost.

The same error appears when a machine cannot reach github.com, which is a network problem rather than an authorization one. See [Troubleshooting](/docs/troubleshooting).

## Where next

- [Projects](/docs/projects) — connecting and configuring a project.
- [Repos on Todos](/docs/platform-git) — the alternative to GitHub.
- [Permissions](/docs/permissions) — the push, merge, and tag switches.

---

<!-- source: https://todos.dev/docs/troubleshooting -->

# Troubleshooting

When a run fails, a red message in the conversation says what went wrong and what to do next. Under it, **Show original error** reveals the model service's or git's own words.

Most failures are not the work being wrong. They are the machine's models or repository not being set up right. Fix the configuration, run the todo again, and nothing you had is lost — the plan, the changes, and the conversation all survive.

The sections below are grouped by the red headline you saw.

## Models and providers

### This model's provider is not configured for the team

The agent's model points at a provider that is not in the team's configuration — never added, or removed. The original error names the missing provider and lists what the team has.

Add that provider under **Resources → Providers**, or assign the agent a model from the picker. The picker only offers models from configured providers.

### The provider doesn't offer this model

The provider is configured, but the model id matches nothing it offers. Two causes:

- **The id is mistyped.** A custom provider's models are picked from the endpoint's list, or typed by hand when the endpoint offers none. A typo surfaces the first time you run a task, not when you save.
- **The model was retired.** Vendors rotate models out without notice — Codex codename models especially. Working yesterday and gone today is normal for those.

Either way, assign a model that still exists.

### The model service rejected the API key (401)

The key is wrong, expired, or lost characters on the way in. Edit the provider and enter it again. The next task picks it up immediately.

### The model service address could not be reached (404)

The request reached the server but hit a path that is not there. Almost always a wrong base URL.

OpenAI-compatible endpoints usually need to end in `/v1`. Use `https://your-gateway/v1`, not `https://your-gateway`, and do not paste the full `https://your-gateway/v1/chat/completions`.

### Couldn't reach the model service

The request never left, or died on the way. This is the machine's network, not your model configuration. Check the machine can reach the service's address, then run again.

### The model service is rate limiting requests (429)

Too many requests too fast. Wait a moment and run again, or switch the agent to another model.

### The model service is out of quota

The subscription allowance or account balance is spent. Top up with your provider, or switch to a model that still has room.

### The model service doesn't accept the developer role

The original error reads like "invalid value: `developer`, supported values are: `system`, `assistant`, `user`, `tool`".

Custom providers never send the `developer` role, so this should not happen for them. If you see it with a built-in provider's key pointed at a relay, use a custom provider entry for that relay instead.

### The model service rejected the request's parameters

The endpoint is not fully OpenAI-compatible and refused a parameter. Common with self-hosted gateways and third-party relays. Try another model, and check the protocol picked for the custom provider.

### The model request timed out

Run it again. If it keeps timing out, switch models or check the machine's network.

### The model's response was cut off

The output stream ended abnormally. Run it again; if it repeats, switch models.

## Repository

### The repository could not be accessed (authentication failed)

The machine is not allowed to fetch this repository. Check the project's GitHub authorization is still in place, and re-authorize if needed.

### The machine can't reach GitHub

A network problem. Check the machine can reach github.com.

### The workspace could not be prepared

The machine could not check the repository out. Expand **Show original error** — git names the step that failed.

### workspaces dir not found

The machine keeps its working folders on a custom path, usually an external drive, and that path is missing. Mount the drive, then `tds restart`.

## Machine and agent

### The task's machine went offline

The machine stopped responding for over 10 minutes, so the run was settled as failed rather than left hanging. A machine that comes back within those 10 minutes resumes on its own.

Bring it back with `tds start`, or run the task again to pick another machine. This applies to your own machines only — a sleeping [platform machine](/docs/platform-machines) is not offline, and running the task again wakes it; one that stays down usually means the team is out of credits.

### The task's machine was removed from the team

The machine was deleted, or enrolled into another team, while this run was on it. Run again to pick another machine.

### The task's machine stopped taking builds

Builds were turned off for that machine while the task was queued on it, and no other machine could take it. Turn builds back on, or run again once another machine is free.

### The task was interrupted by a machine restart

The machine restarted mid-turn and the interrupted turn could not be resumed. Send your message again; the conversation is intact.

### The task's agent was removed

The agent assigned to this task was deleted. Assign another agent and run again.

## Reading errors

The model picker lists what the team's providers offer in general. It does not mean your account can use a model right now: the catalog cannot know that a service retired a model, or that your account was never entitled to it. A model can be in the list and still not run.

Switching models loses nothing. Assign a different model and run the todo again.

When the hint does not solve it, expand **Show original error**. That is the service's own wording, more specific than the translation, and searching that exact sentence usually lands on the answer.

A red line with no hint is an error we do not recognise yet, so its own words are all the information there is. If it repeats, it is worth reporting.

## Where next

- [Model providers](/docs/providers) — where most of these are fixed.
- [Machines](/docs/machines) — offline behaviour and per-machine switches.
- [CLI](/docs/cli) — `tds status` and `tds logs` for the machine side.

---

<!-- source: https://todos.dev/docs/changelog -->

# Changelog

## 2026-09-17

- **App — the board card's menu gains Duplicate task and Copy link, and delete now fires on confirm**: A board card's quick-actions menu can now duplicate a task — the title, description and tags carry over, the assignment too if the task has one, and the copy lands on the board — and copy the task's link. Deletion also changes pace: delete used to hide the row first and wait out the deferred Undo window, the same as close, with the detail page leaving early so a delete could read as if nothing had happened. Delete now confirms first and fires at once — a progress note while the request runs, the todo removed from the list and board and the page closed only once it has landed, and the error leaving the todo in place when the request fails. The list's bulk delete now confirms and fires immediately as well; close keeps its deferred Undo window.
- **App — a task with no plan yet says so**: The plan tab of a task that has not been planned yet used to show the change set's placeholder line — "No diff to show" — which read as if the document were broken. It now reads "No plan yet".
- **Plans — a revision edits the saved plan in place instead of re-emitting it**: Revising a plan used to hand back the whole plan as a fresh rewrite no matter how small the change — every piece of feedback cost a full re-generation, and the entire plan text streamed through the conversation bubble again. A plan-revision turn now carries an edit_plan tool: one call makes one precise replacement (the passage must match the current plan verbatim and uniquely; an empty replacement deletes it), applied to a draft kept on the turn's run and minted as the next plan version when the turn ends, with ordering guarding parallel edits against clobbering each other — a rewrite that touches most of the plan still goes out as a <plan> block. A revision now costs only the passages that actually changed: faster, and a calmer thread.

## 2026-09-16

- **Kanban — a card's right-click or long-press opens a quick-actions menu**: Moving a todo used to mean the card's primary button or a drag. A right-click on a desktop pointer — and a long-press on a touch screen — now opens the card's quick-actions menu, the same adaptive sheet as the header's kebab (a popover at the pointer on the web, a bottom sheet on a phone), headed by the todo's number and title. The menu shows what the phase allows: Edit opens the todo straight into its editor; Complete runs the board's own confirm-and-merge flow where the server accepts it; Close and Delete follow the list rows' deferred Undo window — the card hides at once and the action can be undone for a short while. Delete asks for confirmation first, and stays visible but disabled mid-turn, where the server would refuse it.
- **Task detail — a build's plan can be compared across any two versions**: Version-to-version compare used to be a change-set-only ability — the plan's version menu never offered a second picker, and the diff routes rejected plan documents. The plan's version menu now offers "Compare with another version…" the same way: pick an older version as the baseline and the trigger reads "v3 → v5", with the two plan sources rendered as a one-file line diff in the same change-review view. A plan's versions live in no repository, so the repo-only affordances (opening a file, image previews) stay off — and unlike a change set, a plan version without a commit is still selectable, so every version is comparable.
- **Builds — stopping a turn asks first, and discards the work by default**: Stopping a running turn used to keep whatever the agent had half-done — the machine still committed and pushed the worktree, and the late report anchored it as a new change-set version, so a cancelled implement turn showed up in the version picker and became the base of the next one (plan turns kept the cancelled draft in the model's memory instead). The stop button now asks first, with a "Discard this turn's work — the plan and code go back to the previous version" checkbox on by default. Discarding rewinds the worktree, branch and session to the previous checkpoint before the next turn; the todo settles at the gate the last completed turn left it at (cancelling the first implement after a confirm goes back to confirm rather than an empty review); and the cancelled message stays in the thread as a pending input. Unchecking keeps the old behaviour.
- **Builds — a model-error cut names its cause**: When a turn's final model frame dies after producing output, the cut notice used to be one generic line — "cut off by a model error — may be incomplete" — while the actual cause (say, exhausted quota) sat in the machine's daemon log. The notice now classifies the cause the way a failed run's error is classified and names it, e.g. "cut off by a model error (model service quota exceeded)", falling back to the provider's own words when no rule knows them; the chief's watch wakes and conversation reads carry the same reason. Executors that don't send the detail still fall back to the generic notice.

## 2026-09-15

- **Chief — topic conversations move from the sidebar into a floating window on the board**: The chief used to be a full-page chat reached from the sidebar's Topics section; it is now a draggable floating ball that lives on the board — the chief's own face, an unread dot lighting the upper-right rim, "Chief · C" on hover. On desktop you can drag it to either side of the board and the resting spot is remembered; a click unfolds it into a standalone chat window that moves by its header, resizes from any edge, and folds back onto whichever corner the ball sits in when it closes. On a phone it comes up as the same peek sheet a task rises in. Bare C opens it, on the same terms as N for a new todo (ignored while typing or with a dialog or menu up), and Esc closes the window, deferring to any modal dialog. Topic switching lives behind the window's title, and the chief's settings become a dialog over the chat rather than a page; each topic's composer draft is kept on the device, so closing the window loses nothing. The sidebar drops its Topics section; legacy /chat and chief-settings links (pushes, tds:// links, and old redirects) still land — they open what the link names and hand the screen back to the board. The board guide's creating-a-task step now points at the ball.
- **Landing page — the hero demo's chief moves into the same chat ball**: The homepage demo had stayed on the old layout — five chief topics in the sidebar, each opening as a full page. It now matches the product: the sidebar loses its Topics section, and a chief ball with an unread ring sits in the board's corner, unfolding into a window whose title is the topic picker. The app's launcher ball also wears its unread mark on the rim instead of inside the face. The demo's global search drops the new-topic action and the conversations group. (The demo is desktop-only; below that width the drawer stays behind the header's menu button.)
- **Task detail — the change set can be compared across any two versions**: The change-review view only ever showed a version against the build's base, so seeing what one turn changed meant eyeballing two cumulative diffs. The version menu now offers "Compare with another version…": pick an older version as the baseline and the trigger reads "v3 → v5", the previous version heading the list with a marker, versions without a commit disabled; "All changes since base" switches back. The pinned baseline follows the build as new versions land — a newer head keeps comparing against the same older version — and falls back to base if a rewind deletes the pinned one. A legacy-data fix rides along: very old change documents (from before headSha existed) could read as an empty diff that was trusted and pinned as the base on a merged build — an empty provider answer now always falls back to the real blob, and a backfill stamps the missing commit on older documents so the comparison works for history too.
- **Builds — a cancel lands at once instead of waiting for the next heartbeat**: Cancelling a running turn used to park a flag that the machine only picked up from the model's streaming responses or its 60-second heartbeat — inside a long tool call there is no stream traffic, so a cancel could sit for up to a minute before the machine actually aborted. A cancel now pushes a machine-channel event that advances that step's heartbeat at once: the machine aborts on the spot, checkpoints and reports, and the changes pane stays in step with the Cancelled bubble.
- **Builds — a superseded turn's late report still lands on the build**: When a cancel (or a stale-run sweep) claims the run before the machine has finished aborting, the done report that arrives later with the commit it pushed used to be discarded as "run not owned" — the branch then held work the build never learned about: the diff hash stayed null, the review pane showed the previous diff, and Done reported "No changes to merge". Such a late report is now anchored under the restore mutex: it stamps the run's checkpoint (so a later rewind can target it) and pins the build's changes document and diff hash, unless a newer turn has already landed its own.
- **Builds — a merge waits for a pending rewind to land**: The merge route and the chief's merge tool used to start the merge turn straight off the fast precheck, so a rewind still landing on the machine could ship the rewound-away worktree. Both now run the same physical-restore gate as confirming a plan: the route answers with the restore_pending contract and the client polls through it, and the chief's tool reports honestly that a pending rewind is still landing. The list view's bulk merge goes through the same flow and waits as well.

## 2026-09-14

- **Kanban — a first-visit board guide walks through creating, phases, and local preview**: The six-column board launched without an orientation, and a first visit left newcomers facing a wall of cards with no cue where to begin. The board now raises a three-step guide on its first visit: creating a task — the labeled "New task" button at the board's top right, the board's keyboard shortcut, or simply asking the chief in a topic conversation ("create a task for me…"), which lands it in the Backlog column; phases and advancing — the six columns read left to right as the six phases (a numbered 3×2 legend pairs each phase dot with its name), the card's primary button changes with its state (Start / Confirm / Done, Retry after a failed build, Reply when the agent is waiting on you), the task detail page's top right can confirm the plan, finish, or run again, and on desktop you can drag a card straight onto the target column (the shortcut and drag rows appear on desktop web only); previewing on your machine — the download icon at a card's top right syncs the task branch to a directory on your tds machine, or a copied command checks the branch out in any local clone. Completing all three steps on a device retires the auto-raise — closing mid-guide (✕ or the scrim) does not count as a read, and it does not re-raise that launch; the header's ? button reopens it any time later.
- **Kanban — cards gain a download icon, and the header's new-task control grows a label**: Getting a build's branch onto your machine used to require opening the todo and reaching the detail page's branch dialog. A new download icon at the card's top right now opens that same dialog — both the Sync to machine and Git tabs — straight from the board, and like the action buttons it never starts a drag when pulled. The board header's new-task entry also upgrades from a bare icon to the labeled button used elsewhere (the shortcut hint stays).
- **Task detail — a repo file path in a plan document is now a working link**: An inline-code path that names a repo file used to render as plain code — to check the file you had to find it yourself in the project browser. Such paths now render as a tappable link in the accent color, opening the file in the pane's file viewer right beside the document. The matcher only recognizes standalone relative file paths (trailing line numbers or ./ prefixes are normalized first); commands, URLs, expressions, absolute paths, and machine-local paths are left as plain code.
- **Task detail — the version switcher reports how much each version changed**: The version switch above the plan and changes documents used to show nothing but a version number and a relative time, with no sense of how much a version moved. Each version now also carries its change size — the added/deleted lines as green and red +n / −n counts at the row's end — so you can see at a glance whether a version grew or shrank before switching. The summary rides with the changes document; versions with no diff to read (non-Git repos and the like) keep showing just the version and time.
- **Branch sync — waits for a pending restore to land, and errors collapse into one list**: When a machine workspace owes a physical restore (a message was rewound and the state has not yet realigned), a branch sync used to read the remote branch and target commit right away — possibly against what the machine actually holds. The source and prepare steps now wait until the restore lands (the client polls automatically and the panel stays in its preparing state), and only fail with an honest "can't read the remote branch" when the restore cannot be scheduled at all, say the pinned machine is offline and cannot be woken. Separately, the machine, source, and request errors that used to scatter across the panel in different colors now render as a single bulleted list; and the machine-offline copy simplifies to a direct "your selected machine is offline — start it and try the sync again."
- **Kanban — dragging a card no longer leaves text highlight behind**: On the web, pressing a card to drag it first selected a scrap of its text, and the highlight lingered after the drop. The selection is now cleared before the drag starts, the card's text is not selectable while it is being dragged, and the highlight is swept again on teardown.
- **Landing page — the hero board gains the download icon and the labeled new-task button**: The homepage's demo board had been left on the previous version — cards without a download icon, a bare-icon new-task control in the header. The mock now matches the real product: a download icon on each card's top right, a labeled new-task button in the header, and the ? guide entry beside it.

## 2026-09-13

- **Branch sync — the todo header's "sync to machine" and "branch and PR" become one download dialog**: The todo header used to answer the same question twice — how to get a build's branch onto a machine — with an admin-only sync-to-machine icon and a branch-and-PR modal hidden in the phone's overflow menu. They are now a single download button, on desktop and phone alike, opening a dialog with two tabs. The sync page is a single panel instead of a two-step wizard: the build branch and target commit side by side (both copyable), a machine picker with an online dot, the sync directory, a force switch, and an outcome card that walks pending → running → synced / failed with the reason in full, the fields staying editable between syncs. The permission drops from admin-only to any team member, so anyone on the team can pull a branch down. The Git tab shows the branch and PR state with a ready-to-copy fetch command (and a clone command for platform-hosted repos); submitting a PR from here is gone — a build lands through Done's merge.
- **Branch sync — an outdated client is named by version, and a synced directory is reusable across environments**: When a machine's client is too old to branch-sync, the dialog no longer just asks for an update — it names the version the machine is on and the minimum it needs (0.1.50 or newer), with the same short wording on the claim-time error. A synced directory used to belong to the environment that synced it first; picked by another machine, it was refused as someone else's repo. It is now reusable whenever it points at the same remote, so switching machines is seamless. And when the target commit is already cached locally, a resync skips the redundant fetch and lands sooner — these client-side fixes ship in CLI v0.1.51.
- **Builds — a long-buffered generation is no longer killed by the watchdog**: Some gateways buffer an entire tool call and only forward it once it completes, so the stream stays silent in the meantime — the watchdog used to tighten the idle bounds per phase (30 seconds while outputting), and a retry replayed the very same silence, so one such write could burn the whole retry budget. There is now a single quiet budget per stream — 300 seconds waiting for the first event, 480 while generating — spent on the original request, and breaching it fails the turn with an honest error instead of replaying. Empty deltas don't refresh the timer, and genuine provider errors still ride the automatic retries.
- **Builds — stringified edit arguments with bare quotes no longer fail the edit**: Certain gateways present the edit tool's changes to the model as a JSON string, and the model often writes it back with the quotes in its content left bare, which a strict parse refuses — an edit that should have succeeded failed instead. The executor now parses such arguments leniently (a quote only ends a string where one should), and the edit lands as intended.

## 2026-09-12

- **Kanban — the Progress page becomes a six-column board, and cards drag to move**: The desktop Progress page is now a kanban board along the pipeline — Backlog, Planning, To confirm, Building, To review, Done (last 7 days) — with every column foldable and the fold remembered on the device. A failed build, or a review-phase todo whose build has nothing to accept yet (it was cancelled, or stopped to ask), stays pinned to the top of the Building column instead of getting a column of its own; a queued todo sits on the step its build will run. Cards carry the move that is yours — Start on backlog, Confirm at the confirm gate once the plan is there, Reply when the plan is not ready or the agent is waiting on you, Done at review, Retry after a failure — and on desktop you can also drag a card onto the column that means the same thing: Ctrl/Cmd-click gathers several cards of one column to drag as a batch, the batch applies only to the cards the move fits and reports how many it skipped, and dropping a card elsewhere opens the start dialog pre-set to that path. The phone keeps the same six buckets as tabs. The page is renamed Kanban with its own icon (the sidebar row and global search follow), the sidebar row's idle badge now counts what waits on confirm and review, and the board header gains a new-todo button. The progress route ships each gate row's build doc with the todos, so the first paint buckets exactly the way the live board will, and confirming a build with no confirmable plan yet answers with a clear message instead of an unmapped error.
- **Task detail — one conversation per build, plan/changes and versions in one control bar**: The task detail used to split the build by step, with its own conversation and step nav for the plan step and the build step. A build now has a single conversation — the header switches between Task and Run conversation, and the thread runs the whole way through. The plan and changes docs no longer come from the step nav either: a bar at the top of the doc view switches between them and picks a version, always visible even when there is a single version. The header is simpler too — number and phase state on the left, actions on the right, the layout toggle (doc only / split / conversation only) shown only on the doc view. Legacy plan/build links still pin their doc beside the shared conversation. On web, Escape now closes the docked task panel (unless a modal dialog is open), and the start dialog's button distinguishes Start planning from Start task.
- **Landing page — the hero window now plays the new board**: The home page's demo window used to play a three-tab task list; it now shows the kanban itself — the six pipeline columns at the app's geometry, every column foldable and the strip scrolling sideways past the pane, cards carrying the project, the number, the title, who is on it, how long it has been in the column and the move that is yours. The phone keeps the same six buckets as tabs over the project-grouped list. The demo sidebar and search palette wear the kanban glyph too, and Saltbox gains a planning row so no live column opens empty.

## 2026-09-10

- **Models — DeepSeek V4.1 Flash joins, and DeepSeek's new price sheet lands**: V4.1 Flash shipped today under the canonical id `deepseek-flash`, and the catalog follows it on four providers: DeepSeek itself, OpenRouter (`deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash`), Vercel AI Gateway (same id) and OpenCode Go (`deepseek-flash`) — all hand-written entries, pi-ai 0.84.3 predates the launch. It is natively multimodal (text and image in), keeps the 1M window and 384k output cap, and its thinking levels are low / high / max. Managed inference moves with it: `deepseek-flash` is the new included default, priced off the new sheet at 0.15 / 0.6 with a 0.003 cache read, so a typical task drops from ~280 to ~210 credits. The retired `deepseek-v4-flash` and vision-exp ids still route to V4.1 Flash on DeepSeek's API and now bill at its rates, so agents already on them keep running unchanged; V4 Pro keeps its own sheet until its September 14 retirement. DeepSeek's peak hours also narrowed with the new sheet — the 2x band is now Monday–Friday only (01:00–04:00 and 06:00–10:00 UTC), weekends never peak.

- **Desktop — Windows and Linux releases join macOS**: The desktop app was macOS-only (DMG + ZIP). It now ships Windows (x64, NSIS EXE installer) and Linux (x64, AppImage and deb) builds, with packaging, updates, window behavior and the executor adapted per platform while macOS stays unchanged. Windows and Linux use native title bars (macOS keeps the hidden title bar and traffic lights). On Windows, closing the window keeps tasks running in the tray — reopen or quit from the tray icon or its menu; on Linux, closing asks whether to minimize, quit or cancel, so the window stays reachable on desktops without tray support. Both get a tray icon, with unread counts drawn as an overlay badge on Windows. Shell updates also split by platform: Windows and Linux download automatically and install on restart, while Linux auto-updates only in AppImage form (deb upgrades manually); the web OTA channel stays shared across all three platforms, and web updates and shell updates move independently. Running local tasks needs Git on the system PATH (on Windows, Git for Windows with Git Bash), and the app reports a missing Git Bash before starting the local worker.
- **Models — the retired DeepSeek aliases now read as V4.1 Flash**: The two retired ids in the catalog still said "DeepSeek V4 Flash" and "DeepSeek V4 Flash Vision Exp"; they now read "DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (legacy alias)" and "DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (legacy vision alias)", matching the model they actually route to. The flash alias gains image input, and the vision alias gains the low thinking level and a max_tokens field. Agents already on these aliases behave the same — only the names and capabilities shown in the catalog are more accurate.
- **Executor — an interrupt cuts every bash command in flight**: When the model ran several bash commands concurrently in one turn, an interrupt only killed the last one it started — the first kept running in the background (one user waited out a 9-minute recursive grep). In-flight commands are now tracked as a set and all of them abort on interrupt; the tool boundary only arrives once every sibling settles.
- **Chief — a wake landing mid-turn folds into that turn instead of answering twice**: A watch wake that arrived while the chief's turn was running (most often for the very todo it had just finished or closed) used to sit in the queue and open a fresh turn seconds later — one more message and one more cached-context model call. The drain now decides under the mutex like every other chief input: a turn already running or queued takes the wake as a steer entry (origin 'wake' — never pending, never a user bubble, prompt text only) folded into the same turn, and the reply keeps accumulating into one message; an idle thread opens a turn as before. The gate-park wait also moves out of the drain and into the turn, so entries queued before the workspace and session are ready always open inside the turn's first prompt.
- **Desktop — a sleep no longer hangs the window's requests**: After a sleep every request hung until the app's 15s timeout — the https handler forwarded the window's traffic through the default session's HTTP/2 connections, which stay open here long after Cloudflare has dropped them. Requests now ride the window's own session, which closes all connections on suspend and resume, and a sign-in left in the default jar is moved over once at launch. The todo detail also clears its error line once a reconnect succeeds instead of keeping it after recovery.
- **Desktop — toasts clear the title bar, and the thread title no longer opens settings**: Desktop toasts used to sit in the top-left corner, overlapping macOS's title bar; they now drop below it and leave the title bar clear. The chief thread's title also no longer responds to taps (the settings link is gone), so a stray tap on the blank space around the centered name no longer opens settings.

- **Sidebar — running work comes back into view: a count ring on progress, typing dots on a busy thread**: While any todo runs, the progress entry trades its needs-you pill for a comet ring with the running count at its centre — the drawer row, the rail glyph and the phone's hamburger alike — and drops back to the pill when nothing runs. A thread with a turn in flight wears the typing ellipsis on its far edge, where the row menu sits and still its trigger, and beside the title in the rail's thread picker; a send marks its thread busy at once, and the landing hero feeds its own stream's busy into the list so the row and the composer's stop button agree.
- **App — machines get their own page under Resources, this Mac one row of the list**: Machines used to live in a tab of the team settings; they now have their own page under the sidebar's Resources section, every machine's state read in one place, with a machines row that shows a dot while one is offline or behind. The desktop shell's own Mac shows in the list as its own card, matched by device — a Mac whose registration the shell lost is offered "use this computer" instead of `tds start` — and the add-machine dialog, machine reference cards, search results and the "no machine online" error all point at the new address.

## 2026-09-09

- **Desktop — this Mac becomes a build machine on its own**: The macOS desktop app now bundles the executor and runs the machine on the device itself — an "Use this Mac" button in setup, the add-machine dialog and the machines tab enrolls it, and the machine is online whenever the app is open, no CLI to install. The app and the CLI share one ~/.tds state root and the daemon's pid lock, so the two never run the same machine at once: with the CLI daemon up first the app only watches (reading "run by tds CLI"), and a worker the CLI stopped stays stopped; if tds already holds the machine or registered it elsewhere, the shell refuses before the server is even asked, since enrolling rotates the token out from under whoever runs it. A machine now carries a runner field (cli|desktop) that the web reads for its update and offline copy, and `tds status` names who started the daemon; removing a machine unpins the chiefs bound to it.
- **Desktop — the title bar joins the window, and updates say a release downloaded**: The macOS shell opens its window with a hidden title bar — the traffic lights sit centred in the app's 44px top band, which drags the window and double-clicks to zoom while its buttons still click; the sidebar's top rows clear the lights so the collapsed rail and the page header read as one bar. The update notice changed too: the shell's bundled web build almost never matched the build number each API response carries, so every launch opened with "a new version is ready" a reload could not act on. A stale web build now only nudges the updater to check; what the page announces is the shell having downloaded a release — "a new Todos version is downloaded, restart to install" — once per version, with a restart to hand.
- **App — the project page opens on its files, tasks behind a header tab**: /project/[id] showed the todo list and kept the repo browser on a second route behind a folder icon. The page now opens on the files, with a segmented Tasks | Files switch in the header where the title was, and the project name beside the back control; the tab rides the URL (?tab=tasks) so a refresh keeps it, while a ?phase= link that names no tab still lands on the list. An open file still takes the header over with its name and actions; the old /files address stays as a redirect (ref, dir and path along with it) because agent messages and bookmarks carry it. The header's New action becomes an icon like its neighbours — a list with a plus, since a bare plus above a files page reads as a new file. Opening the files tab on a project from before the field existed no longer crashes.
- **App — a new team's first cards import its own project or skill**: The chief's empty state for a fresh team swaps the two toy examples — the crypto dashboard and the fortune-teller page — for two entry points into the owner's own work: "Import my existing project" and "Import a skill". Both prefill a prompt, and each opens with the chief asking where the thing lives (a GitHub repo or code elsewhere; a repo URL or a pasted SKILL.md), since connecting a repo or creating a skill needs that answer first. The hint under the title now covers both kinds of card; the mini-game stays and takes the sparkles glyph, and the digest stays. The home page hero's new-conversation page draws the same four cards, off the same keys, so the site shows what a new user actually meets.
- **Landing — the hero's sidebar leads with a news briefing and a daily report**: Two recurring conversations join the hero window at the head of the list, the way the most recent ones sit in the app: an AI news briefing (📰) and a daily report across the blog and the shop (📈). Each is a week of the chief's morning posts — the count or the two headline numbers, one line on why, and the file — with no ask and no back-and-forth, which is what a scheduled todo's conversation reads like once it is running. The window still opens on the blog build. They file into two new projects, Wire and Pulse, each holding its one daily todo, with the two schedules on the Schedules page, the ai-news-briefing and daily-report skills on the Skills page, and a staff writer on the team; the weekly data report conversation goes, along with its todo and schedule, the daily report covering the same ground.
- **Landing — the home page argues why it is task-driven, between the hero and the pillars**: The hero claims a task-driven workspace and nothing on the page said why. A new strip now sits between the hero and the pillars, in the pillars' own layout — one lede ("The todo is the best unit of work for collaboration between humans and agents") and four columns, a flat figure each — making the case four ways: better quality (each todo has one clear goal and scope, and the agent's context stays on it), easy to track (a todo is always at a definite stage, so the team's progress reads in one place), easier to evaluate (its own plan, changes, transcript and token record), and built for collaboration (assignable to an agent on any model, or to a person). Copy in all four locales; the figures share a vocabulary with the pillars.
- **Landing — the regression thread is an ordinary day with the suite, and daily threads say the day**: The hero's regression conversation played the suite being set up — the ask for coverage, the first run catching a bug, the suite merging. It now plays the day-to-day once the suite exists: the nightly run reports green on its own, the user asks for a full run on the branch before the merge, it catches a real regression, the chief files the bug to the backend engineer and holds the merge until the rerun is green, and a reader's bug report becomes one more case that gates the fix. The briefing and the daily report post once a morning for a week, but their time marks showed only the clock, so seven mornings read as one; the locale's short weekday now sits ahead of the time.
- **Landing — the chief's conversation becomes the team's front desk, and the store launch goes**: A new conversation, last in the sidebar, is the one with no project in it — the chief as the team's front desk. Three asks in a day, each settled in the same turn: the QA engineer moves to a stronger model with deeper thinking and nothing else touched, the month's token bill by agent with the one todo that cost the most, and a stock-take of the blog's board that closes a todo stuck at confirm for two weeks and sequences a pending one behind the merge it waits on. The chief changes the setting, reads the numbers and tidies the board itself; no dispatch. The store launch conversation retires, while the Saltbox project stays with its board and its scheduled launch.

## 2026-09-08

- **Topics — a topic wears an emoji as its icon**: Every topic's sidebar row used to show the same boxed hash. A press on that glyph, or "Change icon" in the row menu, now opens a picker — a grid of common emoji plus a field for any other — and the emoji replaces the hash in the sidebar, the header, the rail's thread picker, the follow-ups list and search. The thread carries an optional emoji, the PATCH route takes a title, an emoji, or both, and the validator accepts exactly one emoji cluster — flags, keycaps, skin tones and ZWJ sequences included. The web font stack gains the colour emoji families so the glyph renders the same on every platform.
- **App — a new account lands in the workspace, and setup becomes an on-demand sheet**: A new account used to be held at a setup guide until it had a machine, a model and an activated workspace. It now lands straight in the workspace and reads before it's asked for anything — the setup sheet (hosted / own-machine tabs, the activate button pinned in its footer) appears only when a send or a build start finds the team missing a machine or a model, and a team configured elsewhere but never activated is seeded silently on its first send. A chief no longer gets a thread at creation nor on a read: the first send mints it, and the remaining lazy creators (pre-thread aliases, build watches, wakes) serialize per chief so a burst of first requests cannot mint several. The old /onboarding link still redirects into the sheet, and the Stripe return reopens it.
- **Progress — the progress screen lists the whole team's open todos**: Progress used to show only what the user's chief had dispatched plus the todos they watched, so a task started from a project page or by a teammate never appeared. It now lists every todo in the team that is running, waiting on a person, or broken — whoever dispatched it — behind a new GET /api/teams/[teamId]/progress open to any team member; the chief-scoped route, its watch merge and the chief-only build refetch go away.
- **Landing — the selling points become one goal's scroll-driven journey**: Five selling points each played their own loop, with no thread between them. The section is now one story in seven stages — goal breakdown, parallel execution, independent review, live preview, feedback and memory, conflicts and merge, run history — told by a single demo that changes scene as the visitor scrolls: on md+ the demo and a stage rail are pinned for the height of the viewport while invisible spacers below carry the timeline; on a phone the demo is stuck under the nav and the captions scroll beneath it. The demo is drawn from the app's own chrome (the chief thread's dispatch table, the progress screen, a review round in the todo's thread, the file preview bleeding to the edges, the change request that banks a memory, a merge turn that resolves a conflict and comes back for the user's word, the run history list), and the copy matches the hero and the pillars in all four locales.
- **App — a double press renames a topic or a project in place**: The drawer's topic and project rows now take a double press: the first still opens the row, the second swaps its label for a field with the same text metrics. Enter or leaving the field commits, Escape restores, and a blank or unchanged name is a cancel. A topic commits through the same setThreadTitle the rename dialog uses; a project (admins only, as the PATCH requires) goes through a new renameProject on the team context, shown at once via an optimistic store patch and rolled back if the write fails.
- **Chief — the empty state asks for a topic and offers four moves**: The heading is now "Pick a topic to begin", with no paragraph under it explaining what the chief does. The cards for a staffed team with projects are: build the agent team, create a project, summarize progress, show this month's token usage — the product intro and the hand-off search are gone from that list. The hero mock's new-chat page mirrors it.
- **Landing — copy and entry refinements**: The hero lede now ends on the goal you set instead of promising high-quality results. The closing section's title turns from an instruction ("Build your agent team today.") into a state ("Your workspace is ready."), and its button reads "Open Todos" rather than "Start in minutes", on the content articles that share it too. The header's one action was an outline button — meant to leave the primary seat to the hero's CTA, which no longer exists — so it now wears the primary ink, "Open Todos" for a signed-in visitor and "Get started" for a new one. The hero's sidebar hint (a still pill saying the sidebar is live) now brings the app's own attention dot to the spot its arrow names, with the ping ring behind it, riding the pill so the two fade together and gone the moment a touch proves the point.
- **Builds — a repeat stall doubles the watchdog bound, the third fails the turn**: pi's retry replays a stalled attempt into the same prompt, and a relay that only forwards a long tool call once it is complete goes silent the same way every time. Under a flat 120s bound one such write burned the whole retry budget — 8 attempts, 20 minutes, 8× the tokens — and failed anyway, while the chief read the eight repeated preambles as the model looping. The step's attempts now share a stall run: each watchdog fire doubles the next attempt's idle bounds, so a legitimately long generation gets its room, and the third stall in a row is worded outside pi's retryable pattern so the turn fails there. A stream that ends any other way resets the run.
- **File preview — sized delimiters, styled groups and uneven scripts render in .tex math**: A paper's `\big|\nabla I\big|` drew as the literal text `\big |`: the parser knew `\left` and `\right` but none of the fixed-size delimiters, so they fell through to the raw-source fallback. `\big` … `\Bigg` and their l/r/m variants now read the delimiter that follows, as do `\|` and the `\lvert` family. A font command whose argument holds commands (`\boldsymbol{\theta}`, `\mathbf{\hat{x}}`) parses it as math with the style applied instead of drawing `\theta` as text; `\hspace{2mm}` no longer leaks `2mm`, and `\phantom`, `\tag`, `\overset`, `\underset`, `\operatorname*` and `\sum\limits_{i}` parse to what they mean. Subscripts spelled from code points stepped up and down (`Iᵢₙ`, `ₙₒᵣₘ`): only the Superscripts and Subscripts block is cut as one set, and a multi-character run that mixes blocks now goes to layout; a base carrying both scripts no longer spreads them apart. In the .tex projection, TeX's quotes and dashes become their characters in prose (a pair of backticks opened a markdown code span), `\ ` is a space, `\cline` is stripped from tables, and `\textcolor`, `\setcounter` and `\pagestyle` drop their markup.
- **UI polish**: Folded, the sidebar's active row is lifted above the fold, yet the toggle still counted it as hidden — a "show all (1)" whose press changed nothing. The count now comes from the folded list itself, so the toggle only appears when it would reveal a row. The hero demo on iOS no longer stays scrolled after its search sheet closes — iOS scrolls a hidden ancestor to reveal a focused input, leaving the window pushed up; the frame and panes now clip instead of hide, so there is no scroll position to move.

## 2026-09-07

- **Search — a team-wide search palette opens from the sidebar or ⌘K**: Press ⌘K (Ctrl K on Windows and Linux) or pick Search in the sidebar to search the whole team — tasks by title, description or number (`#42`), topics, projects, agents, members, machines and skills — and selecting a result opens it. With an empty query the dialog lists shortcuts: new topic, new task, Progress, Schedules, and the team and resource pages.
- **Topics — a chief conversation is now a topic, marked with a hash**: The thing you open, rename and delete under the chief was a "chat" in one place and a "conversation" in another, and 对话 also meant the exchange itself. It's now a topic in all four locales — Topic, 主题, 主題, トピック — and the sidebar row badge, the follow-ups grouping in chief settings and the topic kind in search all carry a hash icon, while the collapsed rail's chief entry draws the chief glyph (it stands for the chief, not any one topic); the chat-bubble icon is gone. The Chinese settings label for theme moves from 主题 to 外观 so the word is not used for two things. The projects list now reads like the topics list: "New project" moves to the head of the projects group where "New topic" sits above, and the show-all toggle is a plain text row like the topics' instead of a chevron row.
- **Chief — a usage tool answers what a project's builds spent**: Asked how many tokens a project used last month, the chief could only say the data was not there. It can now report the team's token usage and estimated cost, by project, task, model and time range — figures come from each run's model calls and cover task builds and chief conversations, rolled up as a total, by model, by project and as the top todos, with the chief's own threads and builds of deleted todos on lines of their own. Cost is the executor's list-price estimate, and the description says so.
- **Landing — the slogan returns to the task-driven workspace, and Chinese settles on 工作台**: The hero headline, page title, meta description and OG card go back to "The task-driven workspace for humans and agents." (人与 Agent 的任务驱动工作台), with the OG image regenerated from its old two-line layout, and the hero lede becomes two sentences — "Todos is a task-driven workspace. Humans and agents collaborate in one space to deliver quality work." — dropping its max-width to span the container like the headline. In Simplified and Traditional Chinese the product sense is now 工作台 everywhere (it had mixed 工作区 and 工作空间), with 工作区 kept for the file-level meaning — the sandbox disk, preparing a checkout, syncing the local worktree. On a phone the Latin headline's designed line break becomes a space and wraps on its own, so no word is stranded per line.
- **Chat — a running tool shows its elapsed time, and the model stage reads as processing**: The running tool row in an expanded trace now shows how long it has been running. A running message's "Connecting to model" stage becomes "Processing" — connecting named a step the user can do nothing about and read as something waiting to fail, while processing says the turn is under way.
- **Builds — a turn inside a long tool call outlives its replay buffer**: The running tool call was read off the replay buffer, whose TTL was armed once at the first frame — a 12-hour tool call outlived it, and every reconnect after the first hour came back blank. The call now lives in a key of its own beside the live text, each step heartbeat re-arms the turn's Redis state so it expires an hour past the last beat, and the messages route seeds the dated call into the active run while the tool row keeps showing how long it has been running.
- **Models — reasoning models default to a 64k output cap, and a cut turn says which limit hit**: Over an openai-completions relay, reasoning shares max_tokens with the answer, so pi's stock 16384 let a thinking-max turn spend the whole budget on reasoning and end on `length` with no tool call. Custom reasoning models now default to 64000 and the model editor exposes maxTokens. The chief could not have told you: machines listed models by thinking level only, and the chat rendered every `length` stop as "token limit". The catalog now carries context and output limits per model, and a cut turn reads the run's last call against the model's cap — naming the output cap and its fix when that is what hit, the numbers otherwise.
- **Plans — the parallel-build limit clicks through to the plan tab, and slot-taking and cancellation are reliable**: The parallel-build-limit toast now clicks through to the plan tab, and a fan-out batch (a bulk merge) toasts once per distinct failure reason with its click-through kept. Every start that takes parallel-build slots — new builds, the chief's run_builds, the schedule sweep, and confirm / revision / review / merge resumes — now counts and starts under one per-team Redis lock, fixing Merge & Done and AI review moving a todo into a slot phase without the gate, which let a free team run six merge turns on a two-slot plan. A subscription's scheduled cancellation now reads both the legacy flag and Stripe's cancel_at, so a Portal cancellation shows up on the plan tab and in the team mirror instead of going unseen.
- **UI polish**: Bold that ends in CJK punctuation now renders — `**执行顺序：**先并行` used to come out as literal asterisks because CommonMark's flanking rule keeps a `**` that follows punctuation and precedes a letter from closing; the shared normalize pass now moves that punctuation past the closer. An inbox group's heading is its name and count alone, without the hairline it drew out to the right edge, and the out-of-scope heading's count rides the same slot as a project's. Switching chief topics paints a cached thread in the render that moves the id, so there's no skeleton flash and no chance of the previous topic's rows lingering under the new id.

## 2026-09-06

- **Chief — in-flight work moves into a sidebar "Progress" entry and the notification list goes away**: The chief's open todos used to hang off the conversation header; they now live in their own sidebar "Progress" entry — it spins the comet ring while a build runs and counts what waits on you, opening a project-grouped list with In progress / To review / Failed tabs, while settled work stays in the project todo list. The in-app notification list is gone at the same time: a chief reply now marks its own thread unread in the sidebar (the folded section, the rail glyph and the hamburger all carry the mark), the OS badge counts only todos parked on you plus unread threads, and every other notification type still reaches you as push, email or a desktop-shell banner. The progress entry and thread rows no longer spin with a turn either — the count and the unread mark are the whole signal.
- **Models — GLM 5.3, Muse Spark 1.3 and DeepSeek V4 Flash Vision Exp join the catalog**: OpenCode Zen now lists glm-5.3, glm-5.3-flash, deepseek-v4-flash-vision-exp and muse-spark-1.3 (with its contributor-free tier) at Zen's own prices (Flash 0.15/0.5, Vision Exp 0.14/0.28, Spark 1.25/4.25). Muse Spark 1.3 also lands on OpenCode Go, OpenRouter and Vercel, and Vercel gains zai/glm-5.3-flash. Hand-written entries — pi-ai 0.84.3 doesn't ship them yet.
- **Sidebar — conversations fold into a section and schedules move up**: The thread list and "New chat" now nest under a Conversations section that folds with the chat glyph in the collapsed rail, and Schedules move above Projects. The collapsed rail is tighter, with new chat living in the chat glyph's hover card, and the new-conversation row lights up while a draft is open just like a thread row.
- **Landing — the hero demo levels up**: The desktop demo's team gains a second project, Saltbox — the shop beside the blog, with four todos of its own, a one-off Friday launch on the Schedules page, and a conversation that fans listing images, product copy and the storefront out to a designer, a copywriter and a frontend engineer. On narrow screens the sidebar becomes a drawer pulled from the menu button and the window grows a little taller; the sidebar's team row now opens a team page — the chief and seven agents as a card grid, each with its face, model, role, skills and the todo count while it builds. The Chinese headline now leads with "极简产品工作区", and the English headline's two lines land the same width.
- **Chief reliability fixes**: A legacy chief thread id could end in "-" or "_" — which pi refuses — so fresh sessions for that thread threw for good; new threads now use a uuidv7 format and a migration re-ids the legacy ones. A turn you type yourself into a dispatched todo's conversation no longer wakes the chief — each message used to cost one wake-up, one "awaiting the user" report and one push; now only dispatches, relays, confirms, schedules and reviewer-triggered revisions wake it. Auto-titles now price a path or URL by its width, so an unbroken run no longer fills the header whole. And a draft thread's first message no longer vanishes until the turn ends, while a chief reply to the thread you're already reading never counts as unread.
- **UI polish**: Button and icon-button loading now draws the 12px comet ring instead of bouncing dots; the composer's AI-review icon takes the toolbar's tone and size; a message's copied check turns green like every other copy button; and the English sidebar's conversation section head is now plural like its siblings.

## 2026-09-05

- **Models — GPT-6 Astra lands on eight providers**: The catalog adds GPT-6 Astra across OpenAI, Codex, GitHub Copilot, OpenCode Zen, the Cloudflare passthrough, OpenRouter (with -pro and both :batch rows), Vercel AI Gateway (with -fast) and Bedrock, all at 10/50 with a 1 cache-read and 12.5 cache-write, doubling to 20/75 above 272k. A 1.05M window everywhere but Codex, whose backend caps at 872k; Bedrock's openai.gpt-6-astra keeps the +10% regional convention until AWS publishes a price sheet. The entries are hand-written — pi-ai 0.84.3 doesn't ship Astra.
- **Models — GPT-5.6 settles at GA prices and gains the gpt-5.6 alias**: gpt-5.6-sol (Sol) still carried the preview sheet (5/30, 10/45 long) everywhere it bills at OpenAI's own rates, with Copilot lower still at 2.5/15. It now lands at GA — 4/20, and 8/30 above 272k, promotional through at least 2026-11-21 — and Bedrock follows at 4/20 global, 4.4/22 regional; the global.openai.* luna and terra rows had carried the regional +10% numbers and now read the list. openai gains the unsuffixed gpt-5.6 alias, and openai-codex/gpt-5.6-sol takes the 872k Codex window luna and terra already carry.
- **Models — a custom Anthropic relay's max now actually means max**: A custom provider's models carried only the row compat (supportsDeveloperRole:false) and never forceAdaptiveThinking, so on anthropic-messages pi sent a token budget instead of an effort level and folded xhigh/max into high before the request left — the relay showed no level, and a Claude 5 agent set to max ran exactly as high. The custom model definition is now shaped in one place (catalog, step delivery, verify), adding forceAdaptiveThinking when an anthropic-messages model declares xhigh/max — which only adaptive-thinking Claudes have — so max genuinely means max.
- **Landing — orchestration leads, and coding agents plug in over MCP**: The third pillar and its selling point now read "Orchestration" instead of "Chief agent", and the "What is the Chief agent?" FAQ becomes "How does Todos orchestrate agents?". The coding-agent comparison now ends on cooperation rather than rivalry — Claude Code and Codex plug into Todos over MCP and work as team members — and the "what kinds of work" answer drops the task-engine framing and its batch-ops examples for the product workspace and the work it actually carries (a product PoC, shipping features iteration by iteration, clearing a bug backlog, refactors and cross-language migrations, regression testing, and recurring documents like research write-ups and weekly or daily reports).
- **Uploads — attachments ride a dedicated domain instead of failing now and then**: Uploads used to hit the ingress, and ingress-nginx spools a body over 8KB to a temp file — when the upstream answers before the body is fully forwarded, its read hits a closed descriptor and the request dies with ERR_HTTP2_PROTOCOL_ERROR. The bytes now never cross the ingress: every upload asks for a grant first (a small JSON call that runs the membership, type, size and quota gates and signs a five-minute authorization), then the multipart body posts to the dedicated upload.todos.dev (a Cloudflare Worker) which verifies the grant and writes the object to storage. Avatars, project icons and agent avatars ride the same path, plus a commit step that confirms the object before the URL field is written, so a cache-buster never runs ahead of the bytes.
- **Uploads — attachment downloads come off the dedicated domain, reachable everywhere**: Downloads were presigned S3 URLs on the storage provider's own hostname, which isn't reachable from everywhere the app is used. They now come from upload.todos.dev too: the server signs a ten-minute read grant and hands out https://upload.todos.dev/file/<token>, and the Worker verifies it and streams the object from storage. Range and conditional headers pass through as sent; images come down inline, documents as downloads under the display name the viewer asked for. Without a configured Worker the presigned URL is still minted.
- **App — upload progress draws the comet ring**: The attachment thumbnail's upload overlay and the avatar picker's busy state used the generic spinner and bouncing dots; both now draw CometRing, the glyph the chief and todo headers spin while an agent works. The agent and member detail pages, which showed nothing while an avatar uploaded beyond disabling the buttons, get the same overlay on the face.

## 2026-09-04

- **Chief — follow-ups belong to a conversation and can be removed**: The chief settings screen's "Watched todos" and "Timed check-ins" were two read-only lists you could only undo by asking in the chat. They now merge into one "Follow-ups" list grouped by the conversation that armed them — each conversation card lists its timed check-ins (soonest first) and watched todos (newest first), each row carrying a delete button to remove it there and then. A follow-up reports in the conversation that armed it, and the chief can move a reminder or watch into another conversation from the chat; deleting a conversation also clears the reminders and watches it armed. A watch on a scheduled todo now stands across runs — when the todo settles the watch re-arms instead of clearing, so every run reports as usual.
- **Chat — drop files onto the composer to attach**: On the web you can now drop files straight onto the chat composer to attach them (paste-a-picture used to be the only shortcut); paste and drop share one upload queue, and the whole box is the drop target rather than just the text field. Unsupported file types are still refused with a notice.
- **Landing — a "pillars" strip under the hero, two selling points and the MCP nav entry go**: A new strip of four pillars — shared workspace, the agent team, the agent chief, cross-machine runs — sits between the hero's claim and the selling-point demos, sketching the product's shape before the detail; the illustrations follow the page theme with only the chief coloured, to underscore "you talk to one". Two selling-point demos (the chief watching overnight, MCP client access) and the MCP entry in the top nav are removed, trimming the demos from six to four.
- **Landing — the hero demo's sidebar is live**: The hero's desktop mock used to play one fixed conversation; its sidebar now carries one row per page (projects, schedules, inbox, skills, MCP servers, secrets, model providers, …) and clicking a row switches the mock to that page, with the sidebar's section heads on the same row grid. The model line in the pane's header is dropped too, so the mock reads like the real app.
- **Chief — conversation auto-titles stop short**: A conversation's auto-title used to take the whole first line and hard-cap it at 60 characters, cutting long CJK sentences mid-way. It now clips to a budget of ten CJK characters or five words — a CJK character costs one, an English word two, punctuation nothing — and strips the trailing punctuation the clip would otherwise end on.
- **App — a new conversation opens as a draft**: A new conversation now opens as a draft that takes no row in the list; the thread is only minted, titled and listed once its first message is sent, and moving between the draft and a real thread no longer drops the composer's caret or scroll position.
- **App — the sidebar's section heads sit on the row grid**: The "Projects" and "Resources" section headers used to be a line of small text offset from the rows below. They now share the rows' grid — the chevron sits in the same boxed column as the pin button, the label lines up with the row text, and the whole plate is row-height — so a folded section stays in the list instead of floating as a lone caption; a folded section holding the screen you're on takes the active tint.

## 2026-09-03

- **Chief — one chief, several conversations side by side**: The chief used to have a single conversation, so every goal shared one history and queued up behind the others. It now splits into config and threads — each conversation owns its history, session file, digest watermark, rewind state and read cursors, so you can open one chat per goal and run several in parallel. The sidebar gains a conversation list (new, rename, delete, row menu) with a hover picker; "New task" moves to the project header, and cards like confirms and questions belong to the conversation that raised them. Deleting a conversation clears only its messages and session while the chief's charter and memory stay put; wakes and watches carry the conversation that armed them and report there, and the pre-split conversation becomes the legacy thread, created lazily on first touch, so no history, session or backup moves. The landing page's "everything happens in conversation" selling point now reads one goal per chat, run side by side.
- **Landing — a new slogan and a desktop chief window**: The slogan moves from "Effortless Agent teams" to "The minimal product workspace for humans and agents", carried by the landing title, description, hero headline and docs overview in all four locales.
